the proposed constitution establishes the union as a community based on fundamental rights, bases european policies on a code of common values, sets clear and binding objectives and expresses a commitment to respecting economic, social and environmental sustainability. it includes social rights among the classical human rights, binds its external action to respect for international law, simplifies procedures, clarifies competences, extends the scope of community decisions, increases the transparency and democratic legitimacy of the union and also the possibility of participation of citizens. the shortcomings and risks of this text are not few and it is understandable that many citizens, associations and movements which are politically close to us are increasingly dissatisfied vice-president of the commission. the commission agrees that the absence of comparable crime statistics makes the development of an effective eu law enforcement policy more difficult. the commission is working on a draft action plan on eu crime statistics. member state crime statistics experts are being consulted on this draft action plan, which will be presented in the form of a commission communication in the spring of 2005. the two main blocks of the draft action plan are: first, the setting up of appropriate coordination machinery to ensure that member states, the commission and other key actors are part of the process of working towards common data-gathering methods and harmonised definition; the second element concerns the implementation of developing comparable statistics. this will include many different components, to be developed over a period of time, such as definitions of crime types and an inventory of definitions where there is already eu-level agreement. the commission, in close cooperation with europol and other providers and users of eu crime statistics, is developing this project on a step-by-step basis in accordance with member states' ability to provide relevant data. the commission's draft action plan was discussed with european directors of social statistics in september 2004. it was agreed to set up a task force to examine appropriate statistical methods for monitoring crime. this task force will begin its work in may 2005. i should also mention that the commission is providing support for work being undertaken to measure statistically the quality and effectiveness of the judicial process. a seminar on this subject, co-financed by the eu's agis programme, was hosted by the italian ministry of justice in rome in october 2004.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am called upon to present my report on the proposal for a council decision on the exchange of information extracted from judicial records. this is a proposal - as commissioner frattini rightly said - which is only a first step, and it must be taken as a matter of urgency. the aim of the proposed decision must of course be shared by all. the alde group, to which i have the honour of belonging, and the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, which almost unanimously adopted the council's proposal, certainly share this view. the aim is to improve the quality of justice in italy, in europe and in all member states. the concrete action proposed in the proposal for a decision is to share information contained in criminal records. in fact, this sharing was already provided for in the 1959 convention. however, it is technically difficult to make such an exchange of information operational and up-to-date, since the networking of information under the 1959 convention is now once a year and requests are made without a predetermined scope limit. the advantages of the council's proposal are therefore that we have more timely information, while we wait for the computerization to be introduced, to which the commissioner referred, to make information even faster and almost linear. i would like to clear up a misunderstanding for those who have also had a problem with the relationship between data control and confidentiality. the criminal record data are for the convicted like the medical records for the sick: it's a fact. the problem is who uses that data and how they use it. we therefore ask that they be used only by the judicial authorities and between judicial authorities and only in relation to past criminal convictions. that is why the council was right to express the concepts of judicial record and criminal judgment as one of the names to be given to these decisions in advance. i therefore share this work-in-progress which is being done in anticipation of the conclusions to be drawn from the white paper, and i share the principles you have just outlined, commissioner. you said that this decision, and more generally the recommendations which parliament is about to make, must be based on two principles which i think we can all share and which i certainly share with you. the first is that judges' decisions must be implemented quickly. the second principle - you said so - is that there must be mutual recognition and mutual trust in the decisions taken by the courts of the individual countries. thirdly, you said that any assessment of the quality of the work of judges cannot affect the independence of the judiciary. i fully share that view, commissioner, and i would therefore ask you to ensure that the commission gets down to the more concrete facts with regard to these matters. in particular, in addition to listening, i would ask you to specify what you intend to do in the event that a member state shows such a lack of confidence in the courts that, for example, with regard to the european arrest warrant, there are some member states which have not yet done so. we therefore expressly ask that when such matters are discussed the commission should call on the member states which have not yet done so, otherwise it would seem that these member states do not trust the decisions of the other courts and the other member states and that they do not intend to give immediate effect to the decisions of the courts. we also believe that you are right in saying that the independence of the judiciary must be respected: but we also want to know what the commission intends to do when in some member states the members of the executive do not even respect the judiciary and go so far as to ridicule it in front of their own buildings. i believe that the commission's task is also to issue directives and guidelines so that the efforts we are making to improve the quality of justice in europe and in the member states are not being distorted by some member states for very specific reasons.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have spoken about the quality of justice and we have examined the report which seems to be based on the intention of anticipating the provisions of the treaty, in particular article iii-271 on the assessment of particularly serious criminal offences, such as those relating to terrorism. it is therefore reasonable to ask whether we are not going too far in this optimistic view of the quality of justice and mutual recognition of the judiciary. in fact, it is precisely in connection with the sensitive subject of terrorism that very serious events occur, such as the judgment no 2849104 of the judge for preliminary hearings in milan, dr forleo, on terrorism. the ruling, concerning the activities of some accused terrorists (whose names were on the list of both the united nations and the european union), makes a unique distinction, invented by the magistrate, between terrorists and guerrillas. the judge in question writes that "violent or guerrilla activities, even if carried out by armed forces other than institutional forces, cannot be prosecuted even at the level of international law, as long as international humanitarian law is not violated". we are facing a hollowing out of the community's rules on terrorism. we are faced with the betrayal of the civil commitment against terrorism that europe has made, also in this house. this is very serious and i feel i must report it.
mr president, mr vice-president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to add nothing to the reports by mr di pietro and mr costa, which i entirely agree with. let me instead reflect on a contradiction we are faced with tonight. it is common knowledge that only a strengthening of judicial cooperation can make a significant contribution to the fight against terrorism and organised crime, and hence the mutual recognition of judgments, the exchange of information and the harmonisation of procedural safeguards. however, we also know that many member states are doing everything they can to obstruct this judicial cooperation. we therefore believe that its mandate is also to promote - in consultation with the council - a concrete commitment by all the european institutions to this objective. we need more will to do what the european constitution provides for and prescribes, and we would not like it to remain unfulfilled. in the name of judicial cooperation and consultation, mr vice-president, we ask you to speak respectfully but firmly to the italian parliament and the italian government, also because of your past as a minister in that government. italy is the only country that has not transposed the european arrest warrant. what until yesterday could have been simply serious, today - you will agree - is absolutely paradoxical.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i have welcomed and applauded the commission's initiative and mr grosch's work to harmonize the rules on driving licences. we agree on the objectives of preventing fraud in driving licences but above all of activating a tool to facilitate the free movement of union citizens and to contribute to improving road safety. today, european citizens move around and mingle with one another in the streets of europe with great ease. it is no longer sustainable to imagine europeans driving on the same roads with different driving licences, having met too different requirements. this is a classic case where the principle of subsidiarity is essentially inapplicable. i am referring in particular to the streets of my country, italy, during the summer. we cannot think of rules that apply differently because they apply to different people and contexts. the europe of motorists and the europe of road transport is today one of the most successfully integrated european realities, requiring harmonized if not uniform measures. as regards safety and the union's objective of halving the number of road deaths by 2010, if the system for the granting and renewal of driving licences were to contribute even minimally to improving the technical knowledge and skills of drivers and to monitoring the psychophysical condition of drivers, even if it made a very small contribution to improving road safety in europe, it would be welcome. it is for this reason - and certainly not for the sake of unnecessary bureaucratic burdens - that the idea of regularly renewing new licences and of requiring a gradual renewal of existing ones should be emphasized and supported; that agreement should be reached on the idea of combining compulsory training with equally compulsory examinations to ensure the acquisition and maintenance of technical driving skills and that agreement should be reached on the idea of making the issue and renewal of licences subject to the ascertainment of minimum conditions of the mental and physical health of the prospective driver. while common sense calls for uniform rules in all these areas, one area of possible subsidiary differentiation could be the licensing of motorcycles, which is different in the various countries of the union. in this connection, i think it is fair to say that there are countries where access to small motorcycles is earlier than in others. this helps to increase the contribution to the mobility of people in historic centres and can encourage the development of progressive access to the use of increasingly powerful motor vehicles, which is one of the most appreciated features of the directive in question. for these reasons, i think that it would also be possible to allow the equivalence of b and am licences so that motorcycles can always be added to car traffic in the most important historic centres.

member of the commission. one of the main issues in the proposed council regulation laying down general provisions of support for rural development from the eu rural development fund is the review of intermediate less-favoured areas. the commission proposed a revision of the existing classification based, to a large extent, on socio-economic criteria which change over time. it seems that, decades after their designation, some of these areas would not qualify as lfas due to the evolution of their socio-economic features. this was the reason for the critical observations made both by the court of auditors in its special report on less-favoured areas, and by the european parliament. our own evaluation studies also confirmed these observations. the commission cannot ignore these observations and this explains its proposal. from the new period onwards, lfas should be addressed on the basis of objective natural criteria which do not change over time, thereby corresponding to a permanent handicap, such as low soil productivity or poor climate conditions. as a result of the application of the new criteria, areas may no longer qualify for lfa status and farmers located in these areas may no longer be eligible for the intermediate lfa payment. the level of compensation is a distinct issue from the delimitation of a less-favoured area. support is granted per hectare and should compensate farmers for the additional costs incurred and income foregone due to the handicap to agricultural production in the areas concerned. in its proposal for the next programming period, the commission will introduce a distinction between mountain areas and other less-favoured areas with regard to the maximum compensation payable. since mountain areas are affected by the most severe handicaps, the commission proposes setting the maximum amount to eur 250 per hectare, while the maximum amount for other categories is set at eur 150 per hectare.

acting president of the council. madam president, in order to complete the reform of the common agricultural policy decided in june 2003, the council adopted on 29 april 2004 a regulation aimed at partially decoupling support for cotton, olive oil, tobacco and hops and integrating it into the single payment scheme. this reform should enter into force on 1 january 2006. with regard to the cotton sector in particular, it was agreed that, in order to avoid disruption of production in the community's producing regions, support should remain partly linked to the cultivation of cotton in the form of a crop-related payment per eligible hectare. the amount of the aid should ensure economic conditions in regions favourable to cotton growing which ensure the continuation of the activity and prevent the cotton crop from being supplanted by other crops. to this end, the total aid available per hectare for each member state was set at 35% of the national share which producers received indirectly through the vineyard operators during the reference period 2000-2002. the establishment of a base area for each member state, in order to restrict the areas planted with cotton, responds to budgetary constraints and to the specificities of this crop. the setting of ceilings for cotton production is also in line with the international negotiations at the wto, the doha round, where the concerns of the developing countries, and in particular the west african cotton producing countries - much has been said this afternoon - have been expressed for this production sector. the community intends to send an important signal to the wto, and in particular to the developing countries, through this reform.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a directive on unfair trading practices was adopted by parliament at first reading on 20 april 2004. the directive provides for a general prohibition of unfair trading practices and an indicative and non-exhaustive list of general and specific examples of unfair trading practices. the main purpose of this directive is to achieve a high level of consumer protection, as the commissioner has pointed out, and to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market, in such a way as to promote commercial transactions and, consequently, economic growth. the original intention of the directive was based on a sufficiently high degree of harmonisation of consumer protection on the one hand and on the application of the principle of country of origin and mutual recognition on the other. parliament, at first reading, introduced amendments to bring the proposal into better balance by introducing additional consumer protection elements. the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a new legal basis for the protection of the environment, which would allow member states to maintain more stringent national provisions for five years after the directive enters into force. parliament also provided for the commission to report to parliament every five years on the application of the directive and to propose, if necessary, the adaptation of the annex. the most important amendments adopted by parliament at first reading covered a whole range of issues, in particular the inclusion of the definition of vulnerable consumers and codes of conduct, consumer participation and the drafting of these codes and other amendments. the council's common position, which has been sent to us, has of course been examined by the commission and we have considered, at the outset, that we should base ourselves solely on the amendments tabled by the european parliament at first reading, especially in order to avoid reopening the debate on points already experienced during the previous discussions in order not to prolong the time. as regards in particular the so-called country of origin principle, which has been excluded from the proposal, we have considered that it is no longer necessary to ask for its inclusion given the level of harmonisation of consumer protection achieved. it is important to note that the common position incorporated most of parliament's amendments, in particular the notion of the vulnerable consumer, the participation of consumer associations in the drafting of the codes, the inclusion of the definition of improper packaging among the aggressive practices. the council also accepted parliament's proposal for a derogation from five to six years for the application of the legislation. we were satisfied with the compromise reached in the common position, but felt it necessary to reintroduce certain amendments tabled at first reading, which were intended to strengthen considerably consumer protection. in particular, we have proposed to re-introduce safeguard provisions in the following areas: the commission has also proposed that the member states should be allowed to restrict the use of the product to after-sales guarantees, the right to substitute, products similar to those of another manufacturer and designed to mislead the consumer, plus advertising to minors. in particular, with regard to the latter point, advertising is not prohibited but the prohibition of commercial practices that could put children under too much pressure is strengthened. after the draft report had been amended several times, the main points were summarized in a summary report, which safeguards parliament's prerogatives but also takes account of the council's common position. in particular, the amendments concerning the consideration of social, cultural and linguistic factors in the definition of the average consumer in the courts were unanimously accepted by the committee on the internal market; the prohibition on a trader claiming that a product has been approved by a public or private body when it has not been approved; the prohibition of promoting sales by acting as a mere consumer or a non-professional seller; finally, it was considered unfair to give the false impression that the consumer had won a prize when the prize did not exist or was subject to the payment of certain costs. in conclusion, i believe that, with the slight amendments proposed, it is useful to proceed with the adoption of this directive, which will represent, for both consumers and traders in the european union, a step forward in the certainty of the legislative framework and in the protection of the rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the union. i would like to give, and i apologize, one last technical warning: as some issues have arisen in the revision of the translation, the text to be considered is the one licensed by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection (imco). i would like to thank the first rapporteur, mrs fiorella ghilardotti, the commission, the council and my colleagues in the imco committee for the fruitful cooperation which has enabled us, as has already been mentioned, to adopt the report unanimously.
member of the commission. mr president, i should just like to say once again very briefly that this is a very important piece of legislation, not only for the protection of the consumer – i would say more than anything else – but also for the completion of the internal market and to help and protect bona fide traders. it is a realistic compromise; like all compromises, i am sure that many of us would like to certain aspects go further. however, it is a realistic and workable compromise. i agree with mrs wallis that this is a good example of how cooperation between the three institutions can produce positive results for european citizens. most of the concerns expressed today are met by the legislation. i remind you that, in respect to children and other vulnerable consumers, there is still the possibility of stricter measures by the member states based on health, safety, taste and decency. this gives member states room for manoeuvre. the derogation period of six years for higher protection and standards will be very useful. in the meantime, the commission will come back with a report on the application and transposition of the directive, and we will also review every aspect and see how we can take it even further. in this respect, we will see how we can proceed with updating and increasing, if necessary, the list of practices contained in annex i. i must remind you that the list may be modified only by revision of the directive. mr harbour was right: my commitment to parliament is to give priority to enforcement and implementation. otherwise, we can adopt the best laws but, unless they are transposed and implemented by the member states, they will be of no value to european citizens. this will be the commission's first priority and will be reflected in the am very proud that this important piece of legislation comes under my competence. i am proud and very happy and take it as my duty to ensure that it will be transposed properly by the member states.

the commission's statement on the steel sector is on the agenda.
member of the commission. mr. chairman, ladies and gentlemen, the steel industry is a regular item on the european parliament's agenda, despite the fact that the difficult period of major restructuring in this sector, at least in western europe, is over and despite the fact that the european steel industry is generally competitive. it is true that the companies in this sector continue to adapt to competition and to world market conditions. this is why we have seen restructuring in this sector on a regular basis. i would like to stress at the outset that the overall good health of the european steel industry today is certainly based on the ability of the companies and their workers, but also on the general ability to adapt to changing conditions. these abilities have been demonstrated in the past and i'm sure they will be demonstrated in the future. continuous adaptation of this sector, like all industrial and service sectors, is necessary and is the basis for future prosperity. but this fact does not allow us to forget that we have a collective responsibility to ensure that the process of change takes account of the men and women who work in the field. today's debate in parliament is again about the thyssen-krupp plant in terni. the future of the plant was discussed in parliament a year ago and it seemed that the negotiations would have a happy ending, the company had abandoned the plan to close the plant, which had been announced a few weeks earlier, or at least had postponed the plan. unfortunately, it now appears that thyssen-krupp is going to pursue its original intentions. it is not for the commission to assess whether such a decision is economically justified, nor to intervene directly in this process in any way. this is only possible if there is a breach of community rules. there's no evidence of that at this time. the commission has no information at its disposal to conclude that the company is in breach of the standards used in these circumstances. this is either the standards governing employment relations or standards in other areas. to our knowledge, no complaint or notification has been made in this regard. if that were to happen, the commission would of course take appropriate measures in the exercise of the powers conferred on it by the treaty. economically, we can regret the decision on the fate of this factory, this plant, and we must take into account the possible negative impact that decision will have, if it is confirmed, for hundreds of people and the prosperity of the region. we regret that the efforts made by the regional administration staff over more than a year - and i think that these efforts should be appreciated - did not prevent the termination of part of the activities at the terni plant, but this is a free decision of the company and as such must be respected. freedom must be respected, but also the responsibility of the undertaking, which is expressed in particular in the obligation to involve workers and their representatives fully and effectively in the decision-making process. several community directives and national legislation refer to it and the need to comply with it can only be confirmed in difficult circumstances such as these. the undertaking shall also be responsible for any social consequences of a partial cessation of production. the affected workers should probably be reassigned to other activities within the plant. in any event, in accordance with best practice, solutions other than dismissal should be found. where redundancies are necessary, the workers concerned should be provided for through adaptation measures. these principles for the management of restructuring were set out three years ago by the european social partners themselves, on the basis of a mandate from the commission. and that allows me to now address broader issues that go beyond the subject matter that we're not addressing today. the commission has just proposed a renewal of the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. in order to achieve this ambitious objective, in the context of the major economic and social changes we are currently experiencing, we must successfully overcome the challenges of restructuring. the social agenda adopted by the commission two weeks ago also includes measures to help our businesses, our workers and all the other parties involved in the process of change to make the most of the potential benefits and to tackle the problematic aspects. in a few weeks' time, i intend to propose to the commission that it adopt a communication on a general strategy for the european union to manage restructuring and an ambitious programme to increase the potential for economic recovery and to take account of the difficulties involved. the keyword of this strategy will be forward-looking at all levels. the union has developed policies, programmes and instruments to facilitate the adaptation of businesses and workers to the developing world. the commission has also adopted a communication on the implementation of the european year of the environment, which sets out the main priorities for the year. now these different axes need to be better coordinated, new forward-looking approaches need to be developed to anticipate further developments and individual actors need to be able to prepare for the future. i would like to emphasise that partnerships and social dialogue are of paramount importance in anticipating change at all levels, and in particular at sectoral, local and enterprise level. i will propose that the commission, through this communication, instruct the european social partners to carry out a second phase of consultation on two main topics, namely the role of the european works councils as change agents and the application of the general principles established by the social partners on restructuring management. there is also a need to strengthen the social dialogue at sectoral level, which member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you, and in particular the committee on industry, research and energy, for this opportunity to discuss in plenary the issue of doubling the research budget. i start by saying how happy i am that mr locatelli's report on the future of european research received almost unanimous support from the itre committee on monday. this report, which i understand will be voted on in the march part-session, gives us an excellent grounding in preparing the formal commission proposal for the new framework programme. i would particularly like to thank two members of the committee, mr chichester and mr locatelli. allow me first to underline that today's discussion is not just important for research. it is a debate about nothing less than our credibility to reach the lisbon objectives, and is a crucial debate for both our institutions only a few weeks before europe hopefully agrees on the financial means for the next decade. the discussion about the new financial perspectives is a moment of truth and the question of sufficient funding for european research is an essential part of it. this is because research is about knowledge, and knowledge is truly a european strength in global competition. let me explain. some of our trading partners are competing with primary resources, which we do not have. some compete with cheap labour, which we do not want. some compete on the back of the environment, which we cannot accept. the only way for european enterprise to build sustainable leadership is to exploit the knowledge triangle fully: the creation, transmission and use of knowledge through research, education, training and of course innovation. my strong conviction is that european enterprises will only achieve competitiveness and leadership on global markets if we rapidly put europe in the lead as an economy and as a knowledge society. we are strong in knowledge, but we can become even stronger if we pool our efforts in an intelligent way; if we give full emphasis to excellence; and if we use the full research potential throughout the eu - old, new and future. this is what i want the next research programme to stand for. knowledge does not only mean more competitive businesses. it also brings continuous progress to society: progress in fields such as health; preservation of the environment; and sustainable energy supply. all of these rest largely on the progress of knowledge. in view of this, the questions you raised are indeed the right ones. first, will the commission fight for the doubling of the research budget? the answer is yes. in february 2004, when launching the debate on policy challenges and budgetary means of the enlarged union, the commission emphasised the role research will play in building our common future and consequently proposed the doubling of the budget. this was reaffirmed in the commission's communication on the financial perspectives last july and president barroso confirmed the approach to this house last december, when he endorsed the financial perspective that had been proposed by the prodi commission. the last confirmation came in the proposal of the lisbon mid-term review. it spells out clearly the importance of investment in research and development. on behalf of the european commission, i can therefore confirm not only our strong commitment to research, but also that we will do everything to achieve the doubling of the research budget. second, does this doubling take account of the programme's duration, inflation, enlargement and the need to support new actions? i am very grateful for these questions. it is good that we clarify these fully justified issues. fp7 will be the principal financial tool for realising the ambitious objective of driving productivity growth and ensuring competitiveness through knowledge. when i speak about the doubling of funds i am talking about doubling the budget of fp7. this figure does not include related community programmes such as mr gunther verheugen's programme for competitiveness and innovation. our proposal will not simply be a doubling of the initial fp6 budget. it will be built on the basis of the yearly amount to be spent on research during the period 2007-2013 compared to the yearly estimated amount for fp6, and revised following accession. this means doubling on a yearly basis regardless of the duration of fp7. moreover, in the financial perspectives these amounts will be adjusted for inflation according to our general calculation methods. enlargement is one particular issue. in the area of research, enlargement was a reality long before the accession treaty was signed. the current candidate countries also participate in the framework programme. i could, therefore, answer this question by saying that it is true that enlargement has been taken into account, but i would have to add immediately that it is not only in the budgetary figures that enlargement needs to be taken into account. i want this programme to be built on excellence, because i know this is also a strength of the new member states. however in addition, i want this programme to be an enabling one that allows the use of the full research potential in the new member states and creates an active and effective link with the structural funds. additional new areas of research are included and are part of the justification for doubling the funds. thirdly, will the fp7 proposal cover basic research, space research and security research? to be brief, our fp7 proposal will be all inclusive, i.e. there will be no mechanisms outside the framework programme. let me make an important addition here. parliament has highlighted that the complementary objectives of continued reinforcement of existing eu research support, on the one hand, and of support to new areas of research that are of interest to the eu, on the other, require adequate funding. in other words, it would not be possible to strengthen existing activities in an efficient way and, at the same time, introduce widely supported new activities, such as the european research council and technology initiatives, if the research budget was not doubled. doubling will enable us to take a decisive step forward in our overall research policy and in continuing support for the european research area. agreement on the substance of future research activities necessarily implies agreement on adequate funding for these activities. fourthly, how will the commission try to influence the debate on the financial perspectives to achieve the doubling of research funds? in order to underpin the debate on the financial perspectives, the commission will present its proposal for fp7 on 6 april. this will help parliament to give its preliminary reactions to the council that your rapporteur, mr borg is planning to present during the may part-session. it will also allow the ministries for research and science to have an initial discussion at the competitiveness council on 18 april. the commission proposal will provide sound justification for doubling the budget for fp7, based on a detailed and thorough assessment of the impact of the research and development instruments on investment in growth and jobs. i will list the two main reasons for doubling the funding. the first - and, for me, the most important set of reasons - is the need for the european union to be credible in delivering the renewed lisbon agenda on growth and jobs. this includes the need to deliver results on the 3% gdp target for research and development that was mutually agreed in barcelona. doubling the funding is one of the crucial steps towards a more growth-oriented european union budget. the second set of reasons is more specific to research and development spending. firstly, we need high public spending on research and development because it is an important source of r&d investment and for its strong leverage effect on private investments in research and development in the future. secondly, we need more r&d funding at eu level because of the strong added value of european research funding through the critical mass of resources, sharing of knowledge and facilities, strengthening excellence through close cooperation, competition at european level, the coordination of national activities and support for european union policies. let me add to that the fact that we are currently rejecting an unacceptable number of excellent proposals purely because of the lack of financial resources. in addition, there is the need and willingness to fund new category and activity initiatives which demonstrate high value added impact at eu level without, however, endangering existing ones. finally, we should not forget the very simple fact that the costs of research itself are also growing. your fifth question was whether the duration of fp7 should be synchronised with the financial perspectives to ensure a better coordination of planning activities? reaching the goals that i have described will require a long-term view and commitment. that is why the commission will propose that the duration of fp7 should be the same overall as the next financial perspective for 2007-13. we should take stock mid-way through the programme to ensure that fp7 continues to respond to the needs faced by the european economy and citizens. by doing so we will introduce more stability on the one hand, and more flexibility on the other. both factors are needed. i should also like to take this opportunity to underline the exemplary execution rates in the research budget. the current execution rates are close to 100%. we have proved in the past that we can effectively manage constantly increased fp budgets. we are aware that the challenge to managing the doubling of the funds is demanding, but we are determined to provide proper answers. simplification and rationalisation of procedures are greatly needed. administration and modernised management, including externalisation, will provide answers to this challenge. the proposals in the field of research are at the core of the delivery of the new lisbon agenda. that is the only way we can succeed. the time for delivery is now. building a knowledge society is probably the best, and perhaps only, way to sustain the european social model without having to make a trade-off between economic growth, social cohesion and environmental protection. the first and foremost policy priority for the union is thus to strongly support the three sides of the knowledge triangle - research, education and innovation - and to ensure that the triangle operates in the most favourable framework conditions. the change in the structure of the european budget in favour of more growth and competitive oriented expenses in the direction proposed by the commission is thus crucial. this structural change to the european budget should also be followed by the member states in their budgets. the doubling of funds in the european budget should not be seen as compensation for the reduction of member states' efforts. on the contrary, it should be an example followed by the member states. their effort is necessary. if we do not make the effort now, we will have to make it later; but it will be more difficult later and it could even be too late. i mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is very important that the european parliament should reject and firmly condemn all forms of trade and trafficking in human tissues and cells, since this is contrary to the fundamental principle of the inalienability of the human body, and that it should establish a ban on the buying and selling of human body parts. in this connection, i think it is necessary to emphasize the difference between trade and donation. however, we must also state with sincerity and frankness that we must be very vigilant when it comes to donations. in fact, behind the donation there are often motives for profit and therefore exploitation. it is not by chance that the shortage of eggs and sperm has recently been mentioned in countries where the anonymity of donors is no longer guaranteed. it is thus clear that often the giving is not the result of altruistic impulses, but can conceal forms of profit. so i think we have to be very careful, very vigilant and very clear. in conclusion, i would like to emphasize that when we talk about cells it is important to understand the difference between cells in general and eggs. it is important to ensure the legislative freedom of the member states in this regard, as egg donation is not allowed in all countries and is a matter for the member states.

on behalf of the green group in the european parliament. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if we compare this morning's speeches and the resolution on the revision of the lisbon strategy, which we are about to vote on, with the speech by president barroso a few weeks ago, we can only welcome the broad agreement that exists, at least in principle, that the relaunch of the lisbon and gothenburg strategies depends on the indispensable rebalancing of the three dimensions of the strategy, namely the environmental, economic and social dimensions. however, we do not think that this is sufficient to participate, at least in its present form, in the political compromise that is being drawn up. we are of course glad that some of our proposals have been incorporated into the joint resolution, but we believe that there are still some gaps in the text. there is no clear choice of the instruments we must have at our disposal to achieve our objectives and there is no guarantee of the ability and willingness of the commission, as well as of this parliament, to resist those who do not believe in the need for a european government of the economy and who are pushing for a renationalisation of cohesion policies, for a downward reform of the labour market and for further reductions in the union budget. the concern to find a compromise has led to the inclusion of contradictory elements in the resolution, which make the message confusing rather than convincing. we notice some inconsistencies in this text. it is well known that nobody likes to pay taxes, but we do not share the objective of reducing taxes to a minimum and indiscriminately, because this would only increase social inequalities. europe needs tax reform that reduces labour costs and rates in other sectors. the commission has already said this many years ago, but nothing has been done since then and the subject has been dropped from the european debate. secondly, the resolution maintains a very moderate and even ambiguous position on three very important subjects, on which there will be a tough legislative confrontation in the coming months, namely the services directive, the reach regulation and the software patentability directive. the outcome of this comparison will indicate whether the lisbon strategy is merely a return to the old thatcherite recipes or the beginning of a genuine european new deal. mr president, commissioner mccreevy, we think that the bolkestein directive should be withdrawn so that we can start again on the right foot, namely with a directive on services of general interest. we believe, commissioner verheugen, that the reach regulation in its present form is hardly a sufficient compromise between the obviously important industrial concerns and the priority concerns of health and the environment. this is a compromise which the commission, but also the european parliament, must defend tooth and nail against the aggressive lobby of a chemical industry which does not understand that the organisation of an efficient and credible control system is the best way to ensure its competitiveness. finally, i think that to expressly oppose the patentability of software is to say that innovation made in europe is promoted by the freedom and circulation of knowledge and not by the protection of the big multinationals and their monopolies. mr president, there is a fundamental ambiguity in this text as regards the real added value of the union compared with the action of national governments. in our view, this value is given by the ability to invest in growth instruments, which is not reduced to just percentages of gdp, and in non-strictly material sectors, such as education and culture, exploiting renewable resources and sustainable solutions and gradually abandoning sectors that consume and waste resources, such as large infrastructure and intensive agriculture, and that generate high risks to health and the environment, such as nuclear energy, gmos and harmful chemicals. mr president, we will be with you on these choices when we can, but we will be against you and with the citizens of europe when we cannot.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the objectives set by the lisbon strategy cannot be achieved unless the european union radically changes the way it deals with the economic and social problems which characterize contemporary society in europe and the rest of the world. we live in a globalised market economy, which only ostensibly supports free competition. in reality, free competition presupposes equal or at least equivalent starting points through negotiated compensation. this is not the case, and there is no policy for mobility in the various sectors which can help to boost competitiveness and hence employment. to drive the system that has become established with the global market, politics, finance and economics must find new rules than those that governed the market before globalization. only myopia and the inability to understand the consequences of information globalisation thanks to the internet can lead the european institutions to believe that it is enough to meet and set out a series of proposals for them to be implemented. it is not enough to draw up multiannual plans from above. history teaches us that in the last century the economy of a great power was overwhelmed by reality, because of centralized plans that were splendid only in theory. realities are not conditioned by plans, but on the contrary it is the plans that must hold up against reality. at this stage of our society, an economy based solely on unlimited consumerism cannot suffice. the lisbon european council, when it defined the knowledge society, left out certain problems, such as the formulation of rules that would ensure that knowledge is correct and not manipulated or used for illicit purposes. the lisbon strategy will not be able to take the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the lisbon european council in 2000 was a major turning point for european policy in general and for research and the knowledge society in particular. the prodi commission, and in particular commissioner busquin, but first of all italian commissioner ruberti, confirmed in lisbon their plan to create a european research area through a number of actions. this is a key step towards europe becoming the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world. we all know the current gap between europe and its main competitors in this field, namely the united states and japan. the proportion of gdp devoted to research expenditure is 3.12% in japan, 2.76% in the united states, 1.99% in the union of fifteen and 1.93% in the union of twenty-five. we must close this gap and the european research area is moving in the right direction. this project is within reach, but it requires determination to make it a reality, the same determination that was manifested in the creation of the single market and the single currency. the importance of the european research area is underlined by the new competences that the constitutional treaty gives to the union in this area and we therefore ask the commission to act in accordance with the new legal framework. in taking stock of what has been done and outlining future prospects, i would like to stress the importance of continuity between the seventh and the sixth framework programmes. the latter was a break with the previous programmes, setting itself more ambitious objectives and introducing innovative instruments that promote the involvement of a greater number of actors and the integration of their actions. the seventh framework programme, however, introduces a new feature, namely the establishment of the european research council. i also speak on behalf of my colleague, erika mann, who cannot be present for this debate. the european research council is responding to the growing demand from the european scientific community for a new engine for basic research. basic research is crucial for successful innovation and will create european added value. until now, european added value has been defined by the collaboration of research teams in different countries. now, as the mayor report says, it is time to give a new definition of added value, which provides for individual researchers or individual teams in any member state of the european union to be able to compete with all other researchers on the basis of excellence. this is the real mission of the european research council, which must be independent in its scientific assessments, autonomous in its functioning and adequately resourced. i would ask the commission to submit as soon as possible a precise and clear proposal on the structure and composition of the governing bodies of the european research council. the report pays particular attention to the subject of human resources, which is the real strength of the european union. in this connection, it is necessary to create all the conditions for european researchers to be able to express themselves in the best possible way and it is essential to encourage their mobility and to ensure that it becomes a mass phenomenon at all levels of their careers. the two-way mobility between firms, universities and research centres, the harmonisation of working conditions and career progression and the creation of european infrastructures are essential conditions for creating a fertile environment for research. for these purposes, i ask that the marie curie actions be strengthened, which have proved to be effective and promote mobility in the scientific world. i would also like to mention the need to promote women's access to research and their careers, with reference to human resources. we want more women at all levels, even at the highest levels, and we also want gender research. the future of research and of europe also depends on our ability to make science more attractive to young people. a closer link between educational pathways and scientific careers is the precondition for having the quantity of researchers needed for the success of the lisbon strategy. another chapter of the report is technology transfer. the seventh framework programme will have to pay particular attention to technology transfer, coordinating european research policy with industrial policy. the technology platforms and joint technology initiatives are key mechanisms for this purpose and at the same time resources must be increased for instruments specifically dedicated to small and mediumsized enterprises, for which it is necessary to provide for a reduction in the criteria for admission to projects and in general in the bureaucracy, which has often been an obstacle to the participation of small and mediumsized enterprises in research programmes. on this last point, i think we should follow the recommendations of the marimon report and the ormala report, and not just with regard to small and mediumsized enterprises. in conclusion, i would like to briefly mention the thematic priorities, without going into the substance of the individual topics. i think it should be stressed that these thematic priorities reflect the strategic priorities of the lisbon agenda. in this connection, i would like to point out that, in order to implement the lisbon agenda, we must adopt a different approach to spending than in the past, that is to say, we must move from a concept which provides for what we in italy call 'rainy aid' to a concept which favours spending on investments which have a multiplier effect, that is to say, the effect of strengthening growth. finally, i would stress that parliament must not make any concessions on research funding and i hope that the commission will be parliament's ally in this battle. member of the commission. mr president, there could hardly be a better day than today, when this house has expressed its position on the mid-term review of lisbon, to take up the issue of the future of european research policy. let me thank mrs locatelli, the rapporteur, in particular, and all the committee members for the fruitful and intense cooperation demonstrated during this first month of our work together. i would also like to thank everyone present at this late hour for their real interest in and commitment to future european research policy. the commission attaches a great deal of importance to the adoption of the locatelli report. it constitutes the european parliament’s formal position on our june communication and, what is more, will pave the way for preparing the commission’s proposal on the new framework programme to be adopted on 6 april 2005. before highlighting what i consider to be the key elements of the locatelli report, i would like to share with you some thoughts about the general context of european research and our plans for the seventh framework programme. even if some of you heard this during the plenary debate on the question of the financing of fp7 two weeks ago, the context is clear. we want and need to relaunch the lisbon strategy. the intensive discussion this morning on the mid-term review of the lisbon strategy has allowed us to take the measure of the challenges ahead. europe cannot compete on the basis of cheap labour or low social standards. we cannot compete on the back of our environment. we do not have the natural resources to sustain our prosperity; we only have our brains, intelligence and creativity. knowledge, in the broader sense, is our strongest factor of competitiveness in the global, fiercely competitive market place. in europe, we need to become much better at producing knowledge through research, diffusing knowledge through education, and using and applying knowledge through innovation. that means that the knowledge triangle of research, education and innovation must function within favourable framework conditions, which reward the knowledge that is put to work. the commission is already working hard to develop such framework conditions for knowledge and innovation. for example, we will come forward later this year with a revision of the state aid regime, work on fiscal incentives for research and development and innovation, guidelines on cooperation between industry and universities, re-evaluation of the profession of european researchers, and other actions. only knowledge-based growth can leverage the resources that we need to sustain the cost of the inclusive society, with the high levels of care and protection that europeans aspire to. building the knowledge society is thus probably the best and maybe the only way to sustain the european model of society, without having to make a trade-off between economic growth, social cohesion and environmental protection. it is in this same lisbon context that i will present our proposals for the seventh framework programme. as some of you rightly stated during our debate on the oral question on the research budget in strasbourg two weeks ago, fp7 needs to be the framework programme for the lisbon strategy. i could not agree more. i want it to be the programme for the growth and job strategy. the duration of the programme will be seven years, as in the case of the next financial perspectives. but given that we envisage a mid-term review, this allows us more stability, but also more flexibility. both are needed. as regards the structure, there will be more emphasis on themes and less on instruments. cooperation projects, formerly known as collaborative research, will be more focused on industry needs and will therefore be more supportive of growth. i hope that you will all appreciate this new approach. there will be a strong focus on ideas, with actions concerning frontier research in the context of the european research council. the ‘people’ part of fp7 will strengthen the existing and well-appreciated mobility actions under marie curie. the ‘capacities’ part will deal with infrastructures, smes, regions, the research potential of all member states, as well as science, society and international cooperation. as regards the management of the funds, which are to double, i am fully aware of the challenges ahead. but with their simplification and rationalisation on the one hand, and modernised management as well as externalisation of some of the activities – such as the european research council, smes and the mobility actions – on the other, we are prepared to rise to this challenge. turning to the locatelli report itself, a report that will make a significant contribution to the success of the forthcoming framework programme, allow me, firstly, to express my sincere gratitude for all the support you have given until now for the proposed doubling of funds for fp7. this is fully in line with the commission’s proposal for the next financial perspective and firmly defends the proposal to set the eu budget above 1% of gdp. let me make a personal comment here. i really appreciate this support. it is crucial. together we have a real chance to start changing the structure of the european budget in favour of more growth- and competitiveness-orientated actions. the financial perspective debate will thus be the moment of truth for the european union. it will be then, and not later, that we must demonstrate that we are ready to address the challenges ahead of us fully. we should not miss this opportunity to prove that we are ready to invest in the future rather than look to the past. second, you rightly ask for simpler and clearer administrative procedures in order to improve efficiency and reduce the costs for participants, in particular smes and small actors. i have underlined the importance of simplification on several occasions, starting with the hearing last autumn, and i did not forget the message i was given two weeks ago in this plenary. we have been told since fp4 that there will be simplification. it is time to do something. the commission will do all in its power to achieve this and i look to parliament to support it. third, let me thank you for your support for the swift establishment of the european research council: i am using your exact wording. let me underline two fundamental principles that i intend to strive for vigorously: autonomy and scientific excellence. i wish to assure you mr president, ladies and gentlemen, our group has welcomed the commission's proposal and considers the amendments tabled by the rapporteur to be extremely thorough. they are based on a basic principle, which concerns the procedural guarantees to be harmonised and offered to all defendants in criminal proceedings in the european union: if criminal proceedings are organised at european level, the rights of citizens must also be guaranteed at that level. this is an urgent principle because it increases mutual trust between the various judicial systems, without which there is no cooperation. as commissioner frattini has pointed out, these are minimal procedural rights, but they are absolutely essential: the presence of a lawyer at all stages of the proceedings, the translation of all documents, the assistance of an interpreter, and so on. if these rights are not guaranteed, we run the risk of unfair or arbitrary trials. there is, finally, the sore point: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the subject of exceptions, i.e. the possibility urged by some members that member states may not apply these safeguards to particularly serious forms of crime, including terrorism. our group rejects this solution. the compromise reached in amendment no 4 in recital 8 recognizes the need for a legal and ethical assent’ vote, which is not legally binding because the treaty does not allow that, but is certainly a weighty political statement once it has been made by the european parliament. there are both quantitative and qualitative reasons for this. in the first place you have to vote more than 20 months before the accession takes place, which is exceptional. in the case of the eu-10, the period was the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall try to sum up in a few sentences the content of a directive which is of considerable importance to tens of millions of european professionals, but above all to all eu citizens who have to deal with a professional on a daily basis. this very important directive is a key element in the completion of the internal market. within the limits of its autonomy, each state establishes rules and procedures for the exercise of professions, while, in compliance with the treaties, every citizen of the union must be able to enjoy - temporarily or permanently - in any other state of the union the right of access to employment on an equal footing with other citizens of the host state. within the framework of national autonomy, each government decides what the minimum levels of culture and training are for access to individual professions and also establishes who must authorize and control the exercise of the professions. in this respect, in accordance with the treaties, the autonomy of the nations and the principle of subsidiarity, we must harmonize the system. in the past decades, numerous directives have covered this subject, but parliament has now merged them into a single measure within a general macro-system - with due regard for certain specificities and certain professions. the content of the directive is fundamental. i shall mention only a few of them for the sake of brevity. the treaties mention the selfemployed but never define them. for the first time, this directive - albeit in the context of a recital - defines the professions as follows: it is a very important step forward, because by referring to specific articles of the treaty, parliament establishes a definitive framework which is the legal basis for future measures. the directive introduces a fundamental definition - date europe was freed from the spectre of authoritarianism, and that date also marks the beginning of a europe aspiring to peace and social justice. europe was liberated by the resistance of men and women, by the resistance of the partisans who built the institutional and moral foundations of this europe. europe was liberated by those who fought in stalingrad, it was liberated by the allied member of the commission. mr president, the commission would like to present the preliminary draft budget which we adopted on 27 april. this is the last budget for this current financial perspective. in our draft, we concentrate on the main political goals agreed by the commission and parliament, relating to four main policy areas: the relaunched lisbon agenda, security and solidarity, enlargement, and external relations. i will discuss these four policy areas. the core priority of this budget is the relaunched lisbon agenda, which aims to strengthen economic growth and create jobs. the european budget contributes to this objective with three sets of policies: internal policies, agricultural development and structural policies. concerning internal policies, an increase of 2% is envisaged. contributing directly to the lisbon goals, research and development will record an increase of 4.7%. the common agricultural policy also shows a clear overlap with the goals of the lisbon strategy. the year 2006 will be the first year when the funds from direct income will be transferred into rural development spending, which will be boosted to 13.6 %. the european structural funds together will see an increase of 5% and reach eur 44.6 billion. their core tasks are to enhance the growth potential of lagging regions and to increase employment opportunities. added up, all these actions contribute to the goals of the lisbon strategy and account for at least one third of the budget. to come back to the other main objectives of the budget, solidarity and security, the commission proposal foresees measures to improve social and environmental security, ensure fundamental rights and promote active citizenship, especially for young people. the fight against terrorism, improving food and transport safety, and security of energy supply are also among the priority measures, for which the preliminary draft budget proposes an increase of 5%. to conclude on internal policies, i would like to stress that the commission’s proposal leaves enough margin for the budget authorities, and in particular parliament, to increase the budget for those programmes which it considers necessary. but these increases will have to be discussed with the council. the commission is, of course, ready to help and support this initiative. the next priority is to make enlargement a success. the further phasing-in of the new member states is reflected in all the internal headings, with particularly sharp increases in structural – up to 30% – and rural development policies – up to 9%. on the administrative side, this phasing-in is also reflected in the request for 700 new posts. for candidate countries, the commission proposes to budget only the amounts that have already been endorsed for the respective pre-accession strategies. to support these pre-accession strategies, the commission is also requesting 100 new external personnel positions. in the external relations field, accommodating the new 2006 priorities while at the same time ensuring the continuity of ongoing cooperation programmes is not possible within the predetermined ceiling. that is why the commission proposes recourse to the flexibility instrument for the major part of the reconstruction aid for asia. we would like to emphasise that, for the fifth time in seven years, the ceiling fixed in berlin will not be sufficient. i now turn to the global figures of the 2006 budget. the commission’s proposal refers to amounts of eur 112.6 billion in payments and eur 121.3 billion in commitments. the respective increases are 6% and 4%. that represents 1.02% of the european union’s gni in payments and 1.09% of the european union’s gni in commitments. bearing in mind the ongoing negotiations on the future financial perspective, i would like to point out that the commission is asking for what is necessary and sufficient at this stage to finance the union’s policies in 2006. it should be kept in mind that today we are talking about the annual budget. this preliminary draft budget for 2006, which already represents 1.02 % of the eu’s gni in payments, does not take account of the needs of future enlargement to bulgaria and romania, or of the complete integration of new member states, in particular in relation to the agriculture and cohesion policies that have already been decided upon, nor, of course, does it take account of increased investment in growth and jobs, as required under the relaunched lisbon agenda. i am sure that this is going to be an important year for all of us and i can assure you that the commission will strive to help the budget authorities to reach a good agreement on the 2006 budget for the union and its citizens.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i hope that the debate which will follow this evening's presentation will finally be fruitful. i hope that this will be a positive year, but frankly, the starting conditions are only partly encouraging. i am pleased to note that commissioner dalia grybauskaite has found in the draft budget positive answers to some of the questions which are of particular concern to parliament and which are included in its guidelines. i am referring to the modulation of agricultural expenditure in favour of rural development, the increase in heading 2 for regional policy, the lightening of expenditure on youth and culture and expenditure on agencies. i cannot say the same for heading 4 for external actions and for assistance to smes. commissioner grybauskaite told us that the direct assistance to the lisbon strategy covers more than a third of the draft budget. we shall check each case individually, but on first examination it seems to me that the amounts are insufficient. however, even if this assessment were wrong, the reference to the agreement on sustainable development reached at the gothenburg european council is certainly unsatisfactory: there is no competitive growth that is not also sustainable growth. the proposal on external action also appears disappointing. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we would have expected more momentum in general, but our attitude will be constructive. we do not want to make a list of expenditure, we want to defend the prerogatives of parliament and the european union.
i am very surprised to hear in this house that the wto is the instrument for improving and promoting fair and supportive trade. but how can you say such a thing? it is enough to see what the concrete results of the negotiating rounds that have taken place and are taking place have been. but how can you talk about reciprocity between a giant and a dwarf, between david and goliath? how can we expect developing countries to be the winners of this round if we don't change our policies? why don't you get into the merits of the results? why is it not said that subsidies to 25,000 cotton farmers in the united states have starved millions of people in central africa? why is it not said that the trips (trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights) have deprived and continue to deprive 30 million people of aids medicines - the vast majority in africa - and that the imposition of trips on india has halved the number of people in the third world who have access to aids medicines? the impression is that we will be able to liberalize social and health services in the name of a liberalism which will simply end up making these services - controlled by the big multinationals - payable in the countries of the global south, preventing a large part of the population from having access to them. why not talk about the economic partnership agreements? we have discussed them and we have seen their dramatic result in the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly meeting in bamako. through the demand for complete liberalization of trade with the south - in africa in particular - and the reduction of tariffs for those nations, these agreements have helped to destroy them economically, not allowing them to choose their own strategies for a different development. i think instead that we should be fighting for a reduction in the role of the world trade organisation. we should fight to ensure that a whole range of products can be brought under the control of other agencies, such as the united nations agencies, starting with agricultural products and pharmaceuticals. for these reasons our group expresses a strongly negative opinion of the report presented to this house.

the union's information strategy which seeks to improve the techniques and ways in which it advertises itself. however, between these methods and the citizens, a wall of indifference is erected, which is clearly represented by the historical lowest turnout in the 2004 elections: only 45.7 percent. this is not just the result of a bureaucratic communication strategy, but also the result of a europe which is still very far from its citizens, who do not know how it is made, how it came into being, what it is for, who it is for, who it is for, where it leads us, whether it is useful or indifferent to us. let us be clear: this europe is a construction site, so it is clear that its outlines are not yet visible and that it is still, for the time being, the union of the great economic, commercial and industrial powers, much more than a union of peoples and nations. its institutional architecture is strongly affected by this, and the spirit it inspires is not conducive to widespread popular participation. it is from this isolation that the bureaucratic closures have also arisen which have prevented or hindered the relationship with the citizens. in fact, in a europe so differentiated, it makes little sense to have built vertical, one-way information structures from the centre to the periphery, because this has imposed a unified and standardised model of communication which has not been able to work. a model, moreover, in which the citizen must go to seek information and not vice versa: which simply means that no information reaches the vast majority of those concerned. we need a good information centre, a staff of communication specialists, but we also need a decentralised communication concept, which originates in different countries and which conceives this communication from the point of view of different sensitivities and languages. an idea of communication that is not just propaganda. i am convinced that a good way of informing european citizens about europe is to highlight not only the strengths but also the weaknesses, because it is also from these that the real, but unused, possibilities of europe emerge. that is why i think it is useful for all 25 countries
