the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i apologize for having been misinformed about the timetable, but i think i can recover very quickly. we are few in number in this chamber tonight and we are discussing seemingly marginal subjects, but i remain convinced that europe is built on details, and these are important details. the two reports on which i have worked, which are linked to mr koch's report, were basically dealing with small issues: the problem of safety belts, in the case of the koch report, and, in my case, the technical consequences of anchoring and the method of protecting the head of the passenger on buses. it seemed to be a very simple matter, and it is, because we finally decided to follow the commission's proposal not to allow the further use of side seats in buses because the safety belts cannot be fastened with the same certainty and safety as those of the front seats of buses. but we did spot a little problem, which is innovation. in fact, the idea of buses equipped for conferences, i.e. the possibility of sitting around a table even in a bus, is spreading in some countries, especially in germany. this posed the double problem of safety, which must be guaranteed, and the possibility of allowing a different service. the solution reached is to authorize the experiment, allowing the use of these conference buses for five years, at the end of which an assessment of the percentage of accidents is made - which we hope will be as low as possible - already assessed by the commission but in relation to a swiss experiment, so that it can be extended to the whole of the union. this procedure may enable us to decide in a few years' time whether (and how) we should still eliminate side seats where speeds are higher than those normally held in urban centres or whether this new service can be continued. i think that the compromise reached - albeit with greater difficulty than i expected - with the council on the commission's proposal is a good solution and that this will allow us to vote tomorrow with calm and favourably on the reports which have been tabled. i hope my colleagues will do so.
the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the commission's proposal on nutrition and health information is based on the fact that consumers are increasingly interested in having clear information on the nutritional and health value of food and that the agri-food industry needs to respond to this pressing need with clear, accurate and meaningful information that is scientifically supported. all this in a framework of harmonised market rules to enable operators in the sector to compete according to regulated parameters of fairness and equity. healthy eating and good health are an inseparable pair of reference points for consumer behaviour, with consumers now paying much more attention to their diet and becoming more concerned about what they eat and how food affects their health. if this is the behaviour of the average consumer, the agri-food industry has tried to respond to this behaviour by providing more detailed nutrition labelling and information on the supposed or actual benefits of certain foods. the two basic directives in force in the union - directives 2000/13 and 90/496 respectively, on labelling and nutrition labelling of foodstuffs - are not only frequently not properly applied, but also do not meet current consumer demands, since they do not allow data on the claimed health benefits to be provided and do not clearly define the conditions for the use of nutrition information. in addition, the absence of specific provisions at european level has led to a proliferation of indications on food labels, varying in number and type. the member states have themselves adopted autonomous measures and rules to regulate the use of the various indications. the result is a state of regulatory disorder, with different approaches to the same subject, which has led to a state of confusion that produces neither the proper functioning of the internal market nor the protection of public health and consumers. in the face of this legal uncertainty, the need for harmonisation at community level of foodstuffs rules and, therefore, for a regulation voluntarily indicating the basic conditions for food information to be absolutely true for consumers, without prohibiting any foodstuff, is a further step forward in the implementation of the nutrition policy included in the objectives proposed by the commission since 1999 with the white paper on food safety, which expressly states that the union's food policy must be based on strict food safety rules that allow the protection and promotion of consumer health. to these objectives must be added the objective of improving the free movement of the product, since the creation of a regulation will enable operators to be competitive on a fair and just basis in all member states. in the document under consideration, the commission proposed the establishment of a new regulatory framework for nutrition and health claims, authorizing the use of nutrition claims provided that they comply with the provisions set out in the annex, which contains a list of nutrition claims accompanied by specific conditions of use: the use of health claims at the end of an authorisation or notification procedure (if the commission text were to remain unchanged). the commission proposes to establish, through the procedures provided for in article 93 (2), specific nutritional profiles for foods or categories of foods within 18 months, which could be extended to 30 months, and, after consultation of the food safety authority, specific nutritional profiles for foods or categories of foods, and the adoption of a community list of health claims describing the generally accepted role of a food or other substance on the basis of proposals submitted by the member states. in determining the nutritional profiles, the commission consults both food business operators and consumer associations, as well as seeking the opinion of the authority, which is seen to strengthen its role through its participation in the different phases and procedures. it should be noted at this stage that two years have not passed in vain since the presentation, since all the parties concerned - the commission itself, the council, parliament, industry, consumers, the economic and social committee - have made significant progress. the committee on the environment has, however, made a number of changes to the text presented by the commission, notably by deleting article 4, which in my view is a very important article because it defines the nutritional profiles. moreover, the regulation, in its coherence and complexity, would be nothing if this article were not reinstated, which i hope my colleagues will want to do.

the agenda includes the report by mrs agnes schierhuber, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation on support for rural development by the european agricultural fund for rural development (eafrd) (com (2004) 0490) c6-0181/2004 2004/0161 (cns)) (a6-0145/2005).
member of the commission. mr president, at the outset let me apologise for my fellow commissioner, mrs fischer boel. she has been delayed, but will be here before the end of the debate. i wish to begin by thanking mrs schierhuber and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for all their work on this report. the committee adopted the report with 129 amendments. i shall comment only on some of the major points. some amendments reduced the minimum percentages of funding for the three axes, maintained the proposed funding for leader and eliminated the reserve for this approach. this should give more flexibility to the programming priorities of the member states. i understand this need and i also welcome the fact that the european parliament agrees on the need for minimum percentages. this is crucial if we want to ensure balanced programmes that address the wide variety of challenges in rural areas. the commission is prepared to accept the reduction of the minimum percentages. however, i consider that the reduction for axis 3 – quality of life and diversification of the rural economy – from 15 to 8% is too large, and would affect negatively the necessary balance between the axes, i.e. amendments 17, 43, 44, 115, 117 and 118. please do not forget that measures under axis 3, if used correctly, could contribute significantly to promoting economic growth and job creation in rural areas. this is clearly in the interests of our farmers and their families and is closely linked to what we want to achieve under the lisbon strategy. other amendments bring together the strategic and operational planning and reduce reporting procedures to two reports for the whole financial period – amendments 34 to 41. i am sceptical on the first point, since the strategy would precede the operational planning. however, i am prepared to compromise on a reduced frequency of the strategic monitoring, biannual instead of annual. i would stress that robust reporting is essential for accountability and for explaining to europe's citizens the contribution of our policy to agriculture and rural areas. i can in principle accept the main amendments to axis 1 – amendments 54, 63, 65 (in part), 66 and 67. they concern the extension of support for young farmers to subsidised loans, the requirement that forest management plans be a function of the size of the holding, the extension of support to minimum- sized enterprises for the processing and marketing of agricultural products (in the forestry sector, however, the support will remain limited to micro-enterprises), the inclusion of reparcelling among eligible support for infrastructures, focussing predominantly on operations aimed at improving competitiveness, support for the cooperation between actors in the food chain and for the transfer of knowledge. i come now to axis 2, which concerns amendments 73, 79 and parts of 69, 76 and 81. the commission is in principle prepared to accept or partially accept amendments on: the inclusion of the conservation of genetic diversity, the inclusion of payments linked to the water framework directive, not to consider the requirements for pesticide and fertiliser use as additional to mandatory requirements but as part of them, a more flexible approach towards the duration of agri-environmental commitments, the eligibility of high nature value areas among non-productive investments, and the inclusion of loss of income criteria for natura 2000 payments in forestry. finally, some of the proposed amendments are difficult to accept for various reasons. a number of them go beyond the scope of the commission's proposal and existing norms, thus risking diluting their policy effects. others make unnecessary specifications which are already included in more general concepts. in conclusion, i can accept or partially accept some of the fundamental amendments proposed in your report. the other amendments i cannot accept. i wish to thank the members of the european parliament again for their positive and constructive contribution to european rural policy.
i am glad that the commissioner has taken this opportunity to say that the commission is fully aware of the problems facing the rural areas and that it is not possible to avoid the problems of the rural areas. cutting funding to rural development means cutting resources to food security, environmental protection, landscape initiatives, product quality and job creation. the report adopted by the committee on agriculture attaches great importance to measures to support young farmers, who must be encouraged not to abandon the countryside and to orient their activities in a competitive and sustainable way. the effort of mr schierhuber to maintain resources for rural development is to be commended, but the reduction in the percentages of compulsory expenditure on three axes is a cause for concern. it would have been better to have kept the commission's proposal, because lowering rates means giving the member states more discretion in the management of resources and therefore a weaker and less effective european policy. the commission proposal for a reserve to be allocated to the best-spending countries to promote and reward the best projects should also be maintained in relation to the leader initiative. it is also essential that national implementation plans are consistent with the community's strategic objectives and the strengthening of partnerships is an essential tool for achieving these objectives. finally, to turn rural development into a genuine territorial policy, it must be consistent and integrated with all other community policies. these are fundamental elements of the lisbon and gothenburg strategies which we cannot renounce if we want to revive europe, its objectives and its values.
member of the commission. mr president, i should like to thank you for the very valuable and constructive contribution you have made with your opinion on the rural development regulation. i am convinced that your concerns, particularly substantial on the first and second axes, have helped us to understand better the key issues that are important to the european citizens whom you represent in this parliament. i should like to comment on a few of the issues raised here tonight. first of all, the minimum spending rates, which several members mentioned. the commission is open to a balance between axes, leaving more margin to the member states. however, the proposed rate of 8% for axis 3, compared to the 15% proposed by the commission, is too little. please do not forget that measures under axis 3, if used correctly, can contribute significantly to promoting economic growth and job creation in rural areas. this is clearly in the interest of farmers and their families and it is closely linked to what we want to achieve under the lisbon strategy. someone mentioned the need for members to be allowed to prioritise rural development funds on the third axis. they have plenty of room to do this with the minimum rates that we have proposed. but we also need to ensure that member states have a minimum of balance so that they address the variety of challenges in rural areas. regarding young farmers: they need to have the business plan. apart from agri-environment, the commission is not willing to make other measures compulsory. if there is a real problem for young farmers in a member state, the national strategy should address it and propose the appropriate measures. on the other hand, the business plans should not be over prescriptive at this stage. if needed, additional provisions can be included in the implementing regulations. as commissioner mccreevy already mentioned, we also accept the extension of support for young farmers to subsidise loans. i also noted your comments on the grace period for young farmers concerning the minimum standards. let me be very clear on this: there cannot be a blank cheque for young farmers. in principle, they have to comply with cross-compliant standards just as other farmers have to do. however, i am prepared to consider one exception to this principle: when a young farmer takes over a farm that has problems in meeting one standard or another, he can identify this deficit in his business plan and provide for the action needed to address the problems. in this case, it would make sense to give him some time to adapt and during this period we would not penalise him for non-compliance with the standards concerned. on less-favoured areas, you asked me to look at the inclusion of socio-economic criteria and phasing-out periods for areas that have lost their status. the commission proposed a change as regards the present intermediate less-favoured areas. mountain areas and specific less-favoured areas remain as they are today. member states are requested to confirm or to modify their current delimination in their programmes. but for the intermediate less-favoured areas, there is an agreement that we need to change the approach in the light of the criticism from the european court of auditors, which is also shared by this parliament. the commission recognises that more time is needed for this work and that we need to review the criteria we have proposed so far. let us, however, keep in mind that the criteria we use have to be objective to the wto to be able to fit into the green box. in this context, a phasing-out period for the existing intermediate less-favoured areas can be considered. in 2008, the commission will present to parliament and to the council a report accompanied by a proposal in view of an entry into force in 2010. you also suggested we bring the co-financing rate for the outermost regions and the greek islands up to 85%, as is proposed in the cohesion policy regulation. please let me explain why we proposed a slightly different approach. firstly, like you, i believe that the co-financing rates for these regions should be higher. this is why we proposed a co-financing rate that is actually 5% higher for each axis. however, it is good to maintain a certain differentiation between the axes to express the importance that we attach to the second and the fourth. the cohesion policy proposal does not distinguish between axes and, therefore, has no such differentiation. in addition, we offer in our proposal a number of specific advantages to operators in the outermost regions. such specific advantages do not exist under the cohesion policy. some of you mentioned modulation money to be targeted only against the first and the second axis. this is not possible, because once the modulation amounts are made available they are part of the programming as a whole and should be allocated based on needs identified in the national strategic programmes. on natura 2000, we have to strike a delicate balance. rural development funds can, and should, contribute, but they can never be the only source of funding to solve this problem. it is very important for me to underline that there must be other sources so that rural development is not the only banker. i believe that with our new regulation, including the improvements made by the european parliament, we will have a solid basis for our rural development in future. however, we also need the money, which many of you have mentioned tonight. the financial perspective will be the moment of truth. i hope i can count on your support to make it possible to maintain as much money as possible in this very important area. i thank you once again for your excellent work. i heard mr mulder say that the rapporteur had given a vintage performance. i completely agree. it has been a pleasure for me to cooperate with the members of the committee on agriculture.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on tuesday at 12 noon.
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the measures listed in the hague programme, particularly in relation to money laundering, terrorist financing and the exchange of information between the countries of the european union, must be implemented swiftly and effectively. that is one of the aims of the report to which i am a signatory. this objective must be achieved while respecting the confidentiality of personal data - a point which many colleagues have insisted on in this debate - in order to strengthen freedom, security and justice in the european union, which are strongly threatened by international terrorism. terrorism is financed primarily through arms and drug trafficking, and it is clear that transactions by such entities presiding over such trafficking involve official banking and financial institutions. therefore, measures to prevent and counter terrorist financing should focus on these individuals. in this respect, we welcome the commitment made on behalf of the commission by commissioner frattini, whom we thank for his report, and for the timely submission to the european parliament of a proposal for a regulation on the traceability of financial transactions. this initiative, which we welcome from the commission, seems to us to be concrete, rapid and effective. there is also the equally important issue of judicial cooperation. how can a single judge - and in italy there are many who are strongly and effectively engaged in counter-terrorism action - act without an adequate instrument for cooperation and exchange of information? this is a problem that has yet to be solved. i do not wish to underestimate the concern expressed by many colleagues on the issue of the protection of personal data, but there is a priority need: it's about stifling terrorist powerhouses that threaten citizens. we must think carefully about the need for cooperation in the exchange of data, about the need for a tool which will make it possible in real time, with effective measures and interventions, to prevent terrorism, in order to avoid crocodile tears over the hundreds of deaths from bombings or, even worse, acts of biological terrorism. it is clear that the organisation and operational development of terrorist networks require a continuous evolution of means and methodologies, including infiltration. from this point of view, while i have enormous respect for the work and dedication of non-profit organizations, i felt it necessary to emphasize the real danger, already documented by many investigations, of infiltration of non-profit charities by terrorist groups. these organisations should ensure maximum transparency in the management of funds, use only official bank accounts and regular financial channels and make their accounts public also to protect the non-profit sector, which is a pride of european civil society. we must not forget the implementation of the recommendations of the fatf (financial action group), which are of great importance in the development of new rules for bank transfers, which are absolutely necessary to identify the origin and the recipients, who must not hide behind the screen of shell companies. i would like to conclude by recalling the still entirely unresolved problem of financial and tax havens, inside and outside the territory of the european union, which can still provide a protective screen for those international terrorist organisations which threaten the security and tranquility of european citizens.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the first sentence of the national defence strategy document adopted by the united states of america in march 2005 reads: america and the world are fighting a war. this is the ideological premise which has produced in recent years the theorising of preventive war, the violation of individual freedoms, the end of the protection of personal data and the obsession with security. terrorism is a very serious crime that must be condemned and fought. but it cannot be fought with military means and i believe that europe must distance itself from this approach. we need to look closely at the war-terrorism spiral: the military response has made terrorism stronger, we cannot avoid this issue. in afghanistan, the military occupation has led to an exponential growth in opium production, which is being financed by al qaeda. in iraq the war has fuelled the strength of terrorist groups, not all of them of religious inspiration, which is why the anti-islamic obsession must be removed from some of the reports under consideration in this parliament. this obsession also reveals a cultural inferiority to the united states of america. president bush has called on islamic regimes to restrict, monitor and record all donations made by muslims to charitable organizations. however, we cannot regard non-profit organizations, as some speakers in this house do, as the main source of funding for terrorism. we must avoid overly simplistic equations such as: terrorism equals immigration or terrorism equals islam. terrorism must be fought and defeated: the aim is noble, the methods too often improper and sometimes criminal. terrorism is a crime against humanity, but i do not think it is necessary to appoint an international criminal court as the place to judge such crimes, also because it is unacceptable that massacres of civilians in military actions are not judged by anyone. too often mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as a committed europeanist, but also as an italian member of parliament who is also here to represent and defend the interests of his country, i find the so-called juncker proposal unacceptable, which fixes the member states' contribution to the european budget at a meagre 1.05% of gdp. this means, for italy alone, which is a net contributor to the european union, a cut of some eight billion euros a year, which cuts to the bone the funds for employment and justice and cancels almost half the funds for research, innovation and trans-european networks, with the good will of the lisbon strategy. there are too many cuts and too many contradictions. the so-called british cheque should also be revised. the exception, the privilege of obtaining a substantial refund of the contributions paid by great britain, must be abolished. this is a measure that mrs thatcher wanted - if i am not mistaken in 1984 - but which was unfortunately, and incomprehensibly, reaffirmed during the prodi presidency: a reimbursement paid in large part by france and italy. in conclusion, the juncker proposal is yet another demonstration of the abysmal distance between the european bureaucracy and the real needs of the european people.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr gaubert, on his report, which i consider to be extremely balanced and well-articulated. i think this is an excellent contribution to a european immigration policy, which highlights the added value of europe on the one hand and the importance of close cooperation with third countries on the other. i shall now make a few comments on the qualifying points of this report. firstly, as regards the establishment of an early warning system, the commission strongly supports this idea and is drawing up a proposal. it intends to submit a proposal for a council decision on the establishment of a procedure for prior consultation between member states when adopting measures on asylum and immigration by the end of the summer. as regards the link between immigration and development policies, the commission intends to present, also before the end of the summer, a proposal for a communication to develop ideas and concrete proposals to link european migration policy with development cooperation, and in this context particularly sensitive issues, such as the so-called 'brain drain', which is also a highly sensitive matter for the countries of origin of highly skilled labour flows, will certainly be examined. the commission also shares the rapporteur's approach to measures to combat illegal immigration: we are against all forms of trafficking in human beings, of which illegal immigrants are only the victims. we are considering proposals for common rules for the dissemination of best practice in order to combat trafficking in human beings better, seeking to involve third countries more and to promote closer cooperation between third countries and european countries in the protection of maritime borders. the european policy on return also deserves great attention. the hague programme expressly states the need for common european standards in this field. the commission intends to present, probably by september, a proposal for a directive containing common, transparent rules - which we will of course examine together - on return policy, which will take full account of the need to respect the fundamental rights of every person. i do not think that there is any distinction to be made, when discussing fundamental rights, between a legal immigrant and an illegal immigrant: the fundamental right to respect for human dignity applies equally to legal immigrants and illegal immigrants. now, on to the important topic of legal immigration for economic reasons: we are collecting a lot of proposals on the green paper, which you all know, published by the commission last january. a public hearing will take place on 14 june and, based on the outcome of this wide consultation, we will prepare a proposal by the end of this year. this proposal - as i have already had the opportunity to reiterate in this parliament - will be the result of a great european debate. the issue of recruiting and facilitating the recruitment of seasonal and temporary workers is also of particular importance. the importance of economic immigration is widely recognised: i would like to say that, thanks to a genuine european policy on economic immigration, immigration can be an opportunity for europe and its labour market. in some sectors there is even a need for specialised professionals which cannot be met by the supply of european staff. economic immigration, as the rapporteur also acknowledges, is undoubtedly a highly sensitive issue for the member states. i am very pleased, however, to note that the european public debate on the green paper has somewhat alleviated the reluctance of the member states, which in some cases even refused in principle to deal with the issue of legal immigration at european level, and which have now understood that only such a policy can bring about real added value. i would like to conclude by mentioning the two most important issues of integration and the protection of immigrants. as regards the first, you all know that the proposal i made and which the commission accepted is to give special the report by mr fraga, which is excellent in its summary and content, defines the specific features of the mediterranean better than the council's proposal. this specificity implies that while the objectives of community fisheries management must be homogeneous throughout the eu, the instruments to achieve them must be adapted to the specific characteristics of fisheries in the mediterranean. this is to take account of the different biological, geographical and legal situations in the region and to draw on the experience and expertise of fishermen's organisations operating in the mediterranean. a peculiar feature is coastal and artisanal fishing. the majority of the italian fleet's vessels are less than 12 metres long and therefore the difficulties they will encounter in the conversion - so much desired by the community - to other types of fishing cannot be ignored. the coastal and artisanal fisheries must not only be defined but also safeguarded and, in the case of conversion, more compensation and incentives should be devoted to them, so as not to create serious socioeconomic problems for the whole sector. the project also specifies the role of the regional advisory council, a body specifically created to promote the direct involvement of fishermen, as a voice for direct experience in the decision-making process, so that community legislation is increasingly in line with the reality and problems of the fisheries sector. the role of the mediterranean regulation in introducing common rules is greatly appreciated, but that is precisely why it is necessary for all non-european countries bordering the mediterranean to adapt their legislation to the policy of protecting stocks. to this end, it is necessary to strengthen the position of the european community within the major organizations regulating fisheries, in order to spread the european fishing tradition in the main international forums such as the gfcm and ligat. finally, mr president, i would also like to stress the key role of research, since the basis of any good policy is the quality and competence of knowledge of the factors involved. in this perspective, the specific nature of the mediterranean has always been a problem: the problem is not so much the quantity of research but the discrepancy between research and the specific knowledge needs for effective management policy. that is why in future we must insist on the coordination and applicability of scientific research to the action plan.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the statute of members we are talking about must above all lay down the prerogatives of members. it must say who the european member of parliament is, what his rights and duties are, what his immunities are, and transform him from a national delegate into a representative of the european peoples as a whole. in essence, the statute is a fundamental pillar of the european integration process, and it is not adopted to regulate allowances or reimbursement of expenses, but to regulate and enhance the role and function of the member in the european community. uniform economic treatment alone would risk being a discriminatory measure, because it treats different situations equally. those who have given priority to this part of the statute - which i call minor and which serves only demagogically to provoke the emotions of the mass media - have erred and have not understood the profound significance that a new regulation at european level can have. i think it is important that parliament is about to take this decision at a time of crisis, mr president of the union, because it is useful and essential for the credibility mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal we are discussing is intended to establish a community code on the rules governing the crossing of frontiers by citizens. it is part of the treaty of amsterdam, which has incorporated the schengen acquis into the european framework. it is the first real opportunity for this parliament to deal fully with this subject, bearing in mind that the proposal has moved from the consultation procedure to the codecision procedure following the decision of the hague council. this complex and voluminous proposal has two main objectives: first, to consolidate the existing rules on the crossing of external borders, as provided for in the schengen framework; secondly, to develop this discipline further, especially as regards the crossing of internal borders. the proposal is divided into four headings: the first contains the general provisions; the second regulated the crossing of external borders and the conditions for entering the schengen area. the third deals with internal borders, reiterating the abolition of all controls and specifying the cases and the manner in which such controls may be reintroduced; the fourth contains the final provisions. the rapporteur's amendments are largely intended to clarify certain aspects of the commission's proposal in terms of vocabulary alone. these changes are intended to improve the quality of the text and, at the same time, to clarify and simplify the articles. this will be very useful when the border crossing code finally comes into force and becomes a daily use for border guards and authorities. the rapporteur has worked admirably in close contact with all the shadow rapporteurs and the political groups, and has seen firsthand how borders are being crossed today. the rapporteur has, through this continuous dialogue, met all the requests that have been received. in addition, he has had lengthy discussions with the council, with the luxembourg presidency, and it is therefore appropriate that the report be voted on during the current presidency. the compromise reached with the various political groups, in agreement with the council and the commission, was voted on and approved unanimously by the libe committee. i myself made sure before the vote in committee that vice-president frattini's cabinet was also in favour of the report, and i also got a very positive response to each and every one of the amendments proposed. it is precisely because of this general consensus, reached through a complicated series of bilateral and multilateral compromises, that the report should not be modified at the present time and should therefore be accepted in its entirety. having followed its development and having seen in detail that there is no problem, i personally, as shadow rapporteur, suggest that i give my full support to the rapporteur, whom i thank, in a very substantial way, for the valuable work he has done.
i would like to thank mrs trautmann for her excellent report, which deals with the subject of bridging the digital divide. a problem of balanced development, but above all of social equity. information technology is therefore a key element in building a more culturally rich and cohesive society. the information society must be open to all: an element of democracy which takes account of cultural diversity and encourages the participation of citizens, actors and not just consumers. the role of public investment in safeguarding the open nature of information technology is fundamental, for example in ensuring the development of free software and its adoption in public administrations. there is also the question of governance, which europe must address in order to establish a mechanism of control at international level. the mandate of ican is coming to an end. the aim is to ensure the representativeness and legitimacy of the new internet management body by defining a governance with several actors: governments, ngos, the private sector and civil society, each with their own roles and clear obligations. the proposal must reaffirm the common good of knowledge as a means of development and emancipation. unfortunately, there are worrying signs from the council that are going in the opposite direction. the software patentability directive attacks the right to the free movement of knowledge, calling into question the objective of making the information society accessible to all and thus undermining the very foundations of the lisbon strategy.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to remind you that immunity protects parliament and the parliamentary function within it, rather than protecting the parliamentary symbol. as a result, i wouldn't make too much of it. however, as regards our colleague mr marchiani, i am really astonished by the judgment of the french court of cassation, which totally disregards the 1965 protocol on the privileges and immunities of members of parliament, stating that the same rules on this matter do not apply to european parliamentarians as they do to national parliamentarians. the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has repeatedly called for the application of the rules of the protocol on privileges and immunities, which provide that members of the european parliament are to be treated in the same way as members of national parliaments. on this basis the report was drawn up and i recommend it to this plenary session.
the agenda includes the recommendation for second reading, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, on the common position defined by the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the patentability of inventions implemented by means of electronic computers [11979/1/2004 - c6-0058/2005 - 2002/0047 ((cod)) ] (rapporteur: michel rocard) (a6-0207/2005).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, although the common position states that it wants to exclude the patentability of pure software, it does in fact set the conditions for patenting software algorithms. unlike copyright, which protects the entire program, patentability of software would allow a monopoly on the use of generic instructions. with the patentability of these algorithms, in a complex program that is nothing more than a combination of thousands of instructions, you could be breaking hundreds of patents at the same time. for example, linux, which is now used in various programs including by public administrations, would infringe 283 us patents. the introduction of patentability legislation could therefore mean, at least in europe, the end of free and open source software. if software patentability were to be approved, which is strongly desired by us multinationals and european countries that profit from the us monopoly, there would be a shift in costs from the technological and innovative sector to the legal and insurance sector. this would help to exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from the software development process because of the costs and legal complexities. in the end, there would be less competition and less innovation, and european consumers would have to bear higher costs with less choice. the lisbon strategy for the european economic model combines technological innovation, competitiveness and solidarity. however, the council's position is the opposite. the software patentability directive attacks the right to the free movement of knowledge and calls into question the objective of an information society accessible to all. for this reason, the fight against software patentability that we are waging in this parliament becomes a fight for freedom and democracy.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, innovation and research must be a shared heritage and not a privilege for a few. it must therefore be emphasized that the patentability of software as such must be prevented. it is important to remember this principle in order to arrive at a directive which represents a fair balance between unbridled patentability, which risks paralysing innovation and competition, and the need to protect properly those whose invention can really add value on the market. we also call for the patentability requirements to be assessed with the utmost care, taking into account novelty, originality and industrial applicability. this is the only way to avoid the excessive extension of patent rights to the detriment of small and mediumsized enterprises and, consequently, the proliferation of patent litigation, as has been the case for the past 15 years in the united states. in conclusion, we welcome the idea of a fund of financial, technical and administrative support for smes that are oriented towards patentability. in particular, we believe that it is essential to develop a proper european patent system, aimed at ensuring equal access for small and mediumsized enterprises.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in a few years the continuous flowering of ideas in information technology has made it possible to reduce the technological and information gaps. the patentability of software blocks free inventiveness - which until now has been possible even without large capital - in order to defend a monopoly on the use of generic techniques, the result of a very dangerous commercial and political absolutism. this is a serious restriction on freedom of thought and its reinterpretation, which only serves to hold businesses and public administrations hostage to the microsoft lobby and the few multinationals outside europe. patents are a danger to the development of open source software and a disadvantage for all italian and european information and communication companies - which are mainly small and medium-sized enterprises or even micro-enterprises - as well as an economic disadvantage for the diversification of the information systems of administrations. in defence of freedom of scientific research, the right to the transmission of culture and knowledge and the protection of the fundamental rights of the individual, we must save europe from software patentability by opposing the european directive which intends to introduce it and supporting the amendments tabled by mr buzek, mr rocard and mr duff.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as chairman of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, i feel particularly obliged to congratulate mr rocard, mr kauppi and mr lehne on their work, and all those who have been involved in this very difficult negotiation. i must say that the committee on legal affairs has found an acceptable balance which is appropriate to the cultural choices and the debate which has taken place so far in this and other places. i am of course obliged to defend this balance, because it is a result of parliament. like all those who are interested in the subject, i too consider it useful to have a harmonizing directive on the patentability of computer-generated inventions, the aim of which is to eliminate the ambiguities and uncertainties arising from the adoption of different interpretative practices by the patent offices of the member states and to define precisely the scope of protection. however, it must be borne in mind that the adoption of the patentability directive will only be able to stimulate the process of technological innovation if two fundamental issues are resolved. first, the ambiguity about the concept of technical contribution must be removed, which would undermine the effectiveness of the directive as an instrument for the harmonization of patent granting procedures. secondly, a precise and decisive provision on interoperability must be adopted, which prevents the development of standardised solutions in the field of ict. the objective of harmonization cannot be achieved in contradiction with the principles on which the existing patent system is based, which over the years has proved to be an appropriate instrument and an effective incentive for industry, both for small and large enterprises. it is sufficient to consider the increasing convergence between information technology and telecommunications, which makes it possible for firms to offer and use integrated software packages and services implemented by means of electronic computers. in order to allow for the proper development of these new packages, it will be necessary to ensure that the protection conferred by copyright and patent protection can be combined for inventions implemented by means of electronic computers, without the software being patentable. europe must deal with the question of competitiveness, particularly in these difficult times. the patent must help the european economy and the european citizens. if the directive is not clear, it will be to the advantage of non-european companies and we will be failing in our role and our duty towards the lisbon strategy, the much-talked-about new social project and development. as i said, the commission has done a valuable job because it has gone beyond the common position. it is now up to parliament to complete the text by defining the points which are not clear. if this does not happen, the commission will be responsible for a non-sectoral proposal, which is almost impossible to define, instead of a global proposal covering the whole patent, which will satisfy small and large companies. i would like to make this appeal jointly to parliament and the commission.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, patents are an important part of technological progress. however, it is necessary to go back to the original meaning of the pact between the inventor and the company, according to which the inventor has a temporary monopoly on the exploitation of the invention, while the company benefits from the increase in knowledge resulting from the full disclosure of the patent content and thus the basis for further progress. i think it's worth looking at how certain patents are filed. i have the impression that there is a growing tendency to make patents generic, precisely to keep claims as broad as possible. it seems to me that the law firms have taken over and that the loser in this game is society as a whole. this is particularly true of software. in fact, many patents granted are but a vague description of a logical process. for software, i think that copyright protection is enough. that is why i supported many of the amendments tabled by mr rocard, whom i thank for his commitment as rapporteur. i think that the period of protection could be shortened. however, if the inventor is seeking stronger protection, such as patent protection, he cannot derogate from a full manifestation of the invention and must make this the binding basis for claims. this also applies more generally to limit the possibility of legal uncertainty. in this respect, i believe that parliament should play a more decisive role in the framework of the strengthening of the union, including by defining a common position on the european patent office. i am personally in favour of a reform which simplifies procedures, including the adoption of a single language, namely english, through rules which also allow small and mediumsized enterprises to use this basic instrument.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, apart from the official declarations, an amendment has been made to article 2 to allow patent protection to extend to software contained in a technical instrument. this is the gateway to software patentability. it's like one day it's possible to patent scales, notes and chords. it's like if the pentatonic scale were patented, so suddenly a lot of blues music would be in violation of that patent and all the songwriters would have to pay royalties to the people who recorded it. patents have already been applied for ideas that are not new, such as the mouse click to perform an action or the inequality operator in the source code, and for other trivial ideas that are used today in virtually all software in circulation. moreover, if interoperability were to be blocked by software patents and the consumer were to be forced to buy and use products from the same company all the time, there would be enormous consequences, especially economic ones. no company should be able to build a monopoly on proprietary software. a small firm would have to pay enormous expenses to avoid patent infringement and to defend its inventions in court. competition would then no longer be a market issue but would also become a legal issue. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the question of the use of the euro in the community budget. without software patents, europe could keep costs down, stimulate innovation, improve security and create jobs. to the harvard business review headline "patents are smart bombs", i would add "against the possibility of future interaction between different cultures and worlds".
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as radical members of parliament we have been engaged on this subject since the last parliament, in particular with mr cappato, and we are quite clear about the position of parliament which has not been accepted. we are now discussing it again in a situation where, from the extreme right to the extreme left of this parliament, we have interventions - which i particularly appreciate as a liberal - in defence of the market, which is threatened and polluted by the jungle of the bureaucratic army which, following the big monopoly and oligopoly groups, is ready to prevent, with the language of legal bureaucratic power, the exercise of freedom of invention and freedom of the market. i believe that if the amendments tabled by mr rocard and those tabled by myself and 50 other colleagues, including emma bonino, are adopted tomorrow, we will have a strategy and a chance of winning. if not, i agree with mr duff that the conciliation procedure will no longer have to be based on the fact that spain, austria, belgium and italy did not vote in favour of the directive, as they did in may 2004. i am sure that we will be able to change the commission's and the council's positions in the liberal and legal direction.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are two worlds that are asking the european institutions at this moment to have the capacity to draw up a more open and flexible strategy on a subject so important for the development not only of the economy but also of society. they are asking us to correct the common position in the direction of greater openness and flexibility. these are two worlds which are important for europe and its future, namely that of small and mediumsized enterprises and that of young people. many colleagues have already spoken on small and mediumsized enterprises, and i share the call for greater flexibility in order to avoid a tightening of the patentability directive, which could be an obstacle to the activities of small and mediumsized enterprises and become an anti-competitive weapon for their development. i want to remember the waiting of the young. i think that in very few other subjects discussed in this chamber, there has been such a strong mobilization by young people, movements and associations who use software not only to communicate and learn, but also as an activity, as independent work, for a thousand uses halfway between volunteering and new professions, which are managed independently and are also so important for the development of a society with a more open economic organization and more linked to the ability of young people to organize themselves. i think we have often said, mostly rhetorically, that europe is close to the young. today we have the opportunity - the rapporteur. i would like to thank the commissioner and the other rapporteurs. i think we have created a path of work which is useful to all, also in view of the quality of the reports which we are putting to the vote in this house. i am in charge of the european regional development fund, which is certainly the most important of the structural funds in terms of the amount of resources. it was set up 30 years ago and has the key function of correcting the regional imbalances in europe. this is a function which is laid down in an article of the treaty, which reminds us of the needs and requirements of a europe based on solidarity, on the ability to build equal opportunities and conditions of fairness, especially now that we are faced with the challenge of enlargement. the ten new member states represent a great asset in terms of the quality of policy, a great step forward in european history. however, we must also remember that regional imbalances are becoming more pronounced. at the moment, one third of all european resources belong to a geographical area covering only one tenth of the european union, and we have seen a doubling of the number of regions eligible for objective 1, that is to say regions with high structural imbalances and economic difficulties. this is the essential function of a policy of attention and solidarity. if the union were just a free trade area, we could simply redistribute income between the richer and poorer regions. on the contrary - and i thank the commissioner for this - we have the choice of a political, social and economic project to be entrusted to the structural funds, that is, the choice of a development model which serves the european integration process as a whole. it's a development model that makes some member of the commission. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. perhaps i can address the questions in general first. i think we are all generally pleased that these agreements are now in place, that one has already been adopted by referendum and that we can now begin the process of ratification. as i said, this is very important because it can be both a model for other countries and an opportunity for swiss citizens to get closer and closer to the european union. i would now like to return to the legal question, especially since it has been raised. not only the commission's legal service, but also the council's legal service has expressed its views. mr kirkhope, you have said it, but i would like to confirm it again. article 300 of the ec treaty defines four categories of cases in which the european parliament's consent is required for the conclusion of an international agreement: (1) association agreements within the meaning of article 310 of the ec treaty; (2) agreements establishing a specific institutional framework by introducing cooperation procedures; (3) agreements having significant financial implications for the community; and (4) agreements amending a legal act adopted in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 251 or 252 of the ec treaty. in all other cases, the european parliament may only deliver an opinion. the commission's legal service considers that the present agreements do not fall within the above categories of cases. the joint committees set up by the conventions have, in the opinion of our legal service, only limited powers in the context of dispute settlement. i therefore have to support the commission's view, although i have heard that, of course. i would like to say a few words about what mr von wogau has said here and what mr schwab has also mentioned. i think we have heard all the problems and questions you have mentioned, and they concern spatial cooperation, but above all regional cooperation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. of course, they're more bilateral in nature. but i can see that there's a connection here. i cannot propose a solution here, but we are of course aware of this problem and perhaps it can be brought back to the table in discussions with switzerland from time to time. mr president, i have nothing further to add at this stage and i ask that parliament continue to pursue the appropriate procedures.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report on the future of textiles and clothing after 2005 certainly presents a comprehensive picture of the new economic and commercial realities at global level. textiles and clothing are a key sector for the european union and i therefore join mr saïfi in protesting at the absence of the relevant commissioners in this house. the sector, which is made up mainly of small and mediumsized enterprises, is now in great difficulty because of the chinese products, manufactured and sold at very low cost, which have invaded our market. imports from china have increased in a worrying manner, especially after the definitive removal of import quotas in january 2005. as a result, the european union's textile and clothing sector is under unprecedented pressure. more and more often our factories are closing and thousands of workers are out of work. in italy, 24,000 jobs were lost in 2004 and over 66,000 in the last three years. it should be stressed that this problem also affects all those developing countries which used to export their products to europe and which are now no longer able to withstand chinese competition. as a result, factories are closing not only in europe but also in sri lanka, pakistan, morocco and the entire mediterranean area. what can we do? the emergence of new aggressive global players on the world trade scene, in particular china and india, makes it necessary to revise the traditional objectives of community trade policy, which are based on the maximum opening of markets to promote the international projection of european industry. the current situation and its foreseeable developments require a more cautious approach aimed at protecting european industry against unbalanced and destructive competition. the following actions are urgently needed: the commission is therefore proposing that the council adopt without delay - as commissioner michel told us in this house this morning - the proposal for a regulation on the compulsory marking of the origin of products imported into the european union. to define targeted industrial policies to support sectors most exposed to international competition, including through the use of the structural funds; strengthening the trade defence instruments available to european companies, including anti-dumping measures - as was done for leather shoes - and anti-subsidy and safeguard clauses; make the fight against counterfeiting a european priority by supporting the initiatives of commissioner frattini; the commission's choices should be guided by bilateral agreements. if hong kong fails like cancun, there will be no time to revive multilateral negotiations. in conclusion, i would like to call for a review of the position on the new chemicals policy - the reach directive - in particular to ensure the competitiveness of small and mediumsized enterprises.

president-in-office of the council. mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour and privilege for me to be able to present today, on behalf of the presidency of the council, the draft budget of the european communities for the year 2006, as established by the council on 15 july 2005. i should like to begin by saying to members that we, in the united kingdom, have been very grateful and very touched by the messages of support and solidarity in the aftermath of the dreadful terrorist attacks in london. i believe we would all, on an occasion such as this, like to reiterate our determination, as the european union, to tackle on an international level the scourge of modern terrorism as one of the greatest threats facing the world. i believe that the european union has a major role to play in ensuring that we tackle head-on the menace of international terrorism. once again, i thank you very much for the expressions of support and solidarity in relation to those attacks. with regard to the budget, i should like to note the historical importance of the 2006 budgetary procedure. as the last procedure under the current financial perspective, it has a special role in bridging past priorities and future objectives. of course it also needs to provide a measure of continuity and the basis for coherence between two financial perspectives, but it also must offer the prospect of reform and renewal so that future budgets can genuinely meet the needs and expectations of european citizens in the 21st century. that gives the two arms of the budgetary authority – parliament and the council – a very special responsibility. we will need to build on the spirit of cooperation that has developed between us to deliver in 2006 a budget that offers a shared vision for a better future. already, in the short period of time that i have been fulfilling these responsibilities, i value the relationship that i have been able to build with the chairman, rapporteur and members of the committee on budgets, and with the commissioner. whilst it is difficult at this stage of this sort of process realistically to reach any level of agreement, the atmosphere, environment and relationships that are being built are healthy and, hopefully, lay the foundations for a process that will lead to a mutually satisfactory conclusion. to give to a wider audience today an example of the benefits of that cooperation, during the conciliation meeting between the budget council and a delegation from the european parliament on 15 july, we were able to agree two very urgent matters: first, a strategy for financing a significant ec contribution to the rehabilitation and reconstruction of tsunami-affected countries, and secondly, the mobilisation of the european union solidarity fund in favour of slovakia, to help with the effects of a severe wind storm. those are practical, tangible and highly visible actions, important to all of the people that we represent, as well as to the victims of the tsunami. in addition, we were able to reach an agreement on the revision of the financial perspective ceilings for 2006, to permit modulation in agriculture. today i acknowledge that, on the question of the tsunami, there remains a eur 13 million gap but, in the spirit of the cooperation and progress we were able to make back in july, i am still optimistic that we should be able to close that gap in a relatively short period of time. this was a very promising beginning to our relationship. it gives me confidence that, if we retain a constructive and permanent dialogue, and with the assistance of the commissioner, we will be able to find an appropriate agreement on a balanced and satisfactory budget for 2006 by the end of this budgetary procedure. before presenting in some detail the draft budget established by the council on 15 july 2005, i would like to take this opportunity to recall the main principles which have guided our proposals. they are fully in line with the council's budget guidelines for 2006 adopted in march of this year. i think it is very important that we are clear about the priorities and principles which lead and guide the financial decisions. that is as relevant in the context of 2006 as it is in any debate about future funding in terms of the next financial perspective. it is important that we are absolutely clear about the principles, the policies and the challenges which lie ahead for the european union. first of all, the draft budget established by the council shows due regard for the current interinstitutional agreement of 1999 on budgetary discipline and improvement of the budgetary procedure. this is a point which is worth repeating. secondly, council gave particular attention to complying with the annual expenditure ceiling set by the current financial perspective and to leaving adequate margins below the ceilings – where possible – so that there is some room to finance unforeseen events during 2006. thirdly, regarding appropriations for payments, the council has remained committed to a limited and controlled growth consistent with sound and rigorous financial management. the draft budget takes due account of the implementation rates in previous years and the expected implementation rates in the future. it also acknowledges fully the dramatic and welcome improvements in the implementation that we have seen in recent times. securing the right level of payment appropriations for the ec budget is especially important, and i am sure that all members will be aware that national budgets are so tightly constrained. all public spending must be justified and prioritised to ensure continued public confidence and public support. in setting the draft budget, council took an overall approach which kept to those fundamental principles but which also aimed to provide adequate and realistic funding for the european union's various budget priorities. for example, recalling the need for budget discipline, the council increased the margins for commitments under heading 3: internal policies, and heading 5: administration, and created a margin under heading 4: external actions, but without the mobilisation of the flexibility instrument. we believe that this is entirely in keeping with article 12 of our interinstitutional agreement. by carefully targeting amendments, the draft budget was achieved in a way which continues to meet genuine priority needs. the council also took a similarly carefully-targeted approach to payment appropriations across the budget affecting both compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure. while limiting the overall increase of payment appropriations, the draft budget still allows an increase of around 12% for research in light of the priority accorded to objectives set by the lisbon strategy and an increase of 9.8% for structural funds, reflecting improved implementation rates. sometimes, when people refer to the word 'cuts', they are not talking about cuts; they are talking about a different level of significant growth in budget headings, and yet sometimes the council has been accused of proposing cuts. we are not proposing cuts in the vast majority of budget headings; we are talking about sustained and stable growth, but not necessarily to the level that others consider to be the best way forward. i now want to move on to setting out the draft budget for 2006 in more detail. the 2006 draft budget establishes commitment appropriations at eur 120.8 billion, an increase of 3.7% over the 2005 budget, and it establishes payment appropriations at eur 111.4 million, 4.9% more than the 2005 budget, and payments correspond to 1.01% of community gni. hopefully, you will have all received a comprehensive explanatory memorandum on the draft budget. i do not intend to bore you now with a line-by-line explanation – unless you really want me to, and i suspect you do not. however, i should draw your attention to the key points affecting the various budget headings of the financial perspective. i will begin with heading 1, concerning agricultural expenditure. let me stress my appreciation for the agreement that we reached to adjust the financial perspective ceiling for 2006. that will allow a transfer of eur 655 million from market expenditure in subheading 1a to rural development in subheading 1b. regarding appropriations, the council has made an across-the-board reduction in commitments and payments of eur 150 million, affecting budget lines in subheading 1a greater than eur 50 million. that reduction is designed to take account of under-implementation in recent years. however, the council's position will be reviewed – and this is an important point – in the light of updated forecasts due in the autumn amending letter to the pdb. i must stress that this modest reduction is in line with the council's overall approach of controlled growth of payment appropriations, which should apply to both compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure. the council has accepted in full the amount proposed by the commission for subheading 1b, where it believes the implementation is more effective. turning to heading 2, on structural operations, the council has adopted the commitment appropriations proposed by the commission consistent with the european council's conclusions of march 1999 in berlin and of december 2002 in copenhagen. payment appropriations have been reduced across the board by a total of eur 150 million, which reflects the council's view of the expected implementation rate and is based on past evidence of implementation shortfalls, taking full account of the significant and welcome improvements achieved recently. the reduction is applied to both structural funds and to community initiatives. in heading 3, on internal policies, the council accepted the amounts proposed in commitments for multiannual programmes adopted under the codecision procedure, as agreed following enlargement, as well as the specific amounts relating to copenhagen commitments. however, the council limited commitment appropriations for some budget lines that are not based on multiannual programmes such as those based on commission prerogatives, pilot projects and preparatory actions. those decisions followed the council's examinations of activity statements, which are fast becoming a very important analytical tool. in addition, the council limited the increase of appropriation for the subsidies of certain decentralised agencies. it is right that established agencies should face the same budgetary rigour that we expect of central institutions and, indeed, of our own domestic organisations. however, it is also fair to allow more significant increases for new and developing agencies. the draft budget seeks to make that distinction. in considering the level of payment appropriations for heading 3, council took full account of the need to increase payments, especially for the important research lines that will help to underpin the very important – the central – lisbon reform agenda. however, the council could not ignore the past implementation record for this heading. we suggest there is limited capacity to absorb increases effectively and efficiently. in this environment, the council believes that it would be irresponsible to budget the huge increases proposed in the pdb of nearly 12% across that particular heading. the council has reduced the overall increase to a more manageable and realistic 5%. but, very importantly, we should be aware that the draft budget still permits a very substantial increase – and i want to reiterate this – of nearly 12% for research lines, which reflects the priority accorded to this very important policy area. the council has provided adequate funding for heading 3 and established a sensible margin of eur 210 million under the ceiling. i am sure that parliament will want to keep the same budget discipline principles in mind when considering priorities for this heading. i want to move now from heading 3 to heading 4: external actions. the council was concerned to respect the ceilings of the financial perspective. consistent with the interinstitutional agreement, the council took the view that all possibilities for re-allocation must be exhausted prior to a proposal to deploy the flexibility instrument. you will not be surprised to hear that the council did not share the commission's view that re-allocation had been exhausted in the pdb. the council fully supported the community pledges and consequential budget proposals for the reconstruction needs in tsunami-affected countries and in iraq, and it respected the reference amounts for codecided programmes. it also accepted the amount for cfsp, as proposed in the pdb. however, the council took the view that there was still scope to bring total expenditure within the budget ceiling and achieved this by a very modest across-the-board reduction in commitments to the remaining chapters, including, for example, for international fisheries agreements. a slightly smaller reduction was applied to afghanistan, which still allows the community to meet its multiannual pledge for reconstruction assistance. after these adjustments, the margin available under heading 4 is eur 41.65 million, which should allow the financing of the consequences of the forthcoming sugar reforms along the lines we expect the commission to propose. again, we share a common belief that it is absolutely essential to make a success of sugar reform. i hope that we will be able to reach agreement on the final amount for the cfsp budget and the international fisheries agreements in the course of the second reading of the budget for 2006, as foreseen in the interinstitutional agreement. you can rest assured that we, the presidency, will make every effort to provide the appropriate information about cfsp to the european parliament on time and in an appropriate form. i am sure you would agree that much progress has been made in recent times in relation to that particular issue. moving on now to heading 5, on administrative expenditure, the draft budget aims to respect the ceiling of the financial perspective once again and set an adequate margin for unforeseen events. with this in mind, the council established a margin of eur 130 million, to be achieved through savings in operating costs from interinstitutional cooperation and from budget reductions, to reflect the current vacancy rate for the various institutions. the council's approach was objective and pragmatic, although we can never expect any institution to be entirely satisfied inevitably by the outcome of our analysis. the council accepted the vast majority of the new posts requested by the institutions for enlargement, pre-enlargement and new tasks. however, it is true that we applied a modest reduction to take account of the significant delay in recruitment for posts granted in previous years. the council expressed deep concern about recruitment delays and about the need – the centrality – for there to be geographical balance following enlargement. i know that parliament shares these concerns. it is regrettable that, due to time constraints, we could not agree a jointly-worded statement on this issue on 15 july, but i have every reason to believe that we can still reach such an agreement which would make it absolutely clear that parliament and the council are as one in terms of recruitment and retention, of human resource policies. we have recently received a paper from the commissioner, which we will be considering over the next few weeks, to inform our position on the question of administration and more specifically of posts. moving on now to heading 7, the pre-accession strategy, the council accepted the commitment appropriations proposed by the commission. however we limited the increase for payment appropriations for some budget lines, again taking into account past implementation rates. finally, as regards heading 8, on compensations, the council accepted the full amounts proposed by the commission in the pdb, which will help ensure that the conclusions of the copenhagen european council as regards new member states are properly fulfilled. we believe that this draft budget adequately responds to the european union's various priorities, making the finances available, but it also respects the important principle of budgetary discipline and sound management of which we – the council and parliament – are joint custodians. we meet today in an environment where it is more important than ever that we rebuild, that we strengthen the relationship between the european union, its institutions and the people of europe. central to that relationship is the credibility of the way we do our business. key to that credibility is the way that we manage our finances, to demonstrate that we are efficient, that we are prudent, but also that we jointly spend money in a way that adds value to the everyday quality of life of the people who live in the european union. we have to close the gap between rhetoric and reality, because one of our great challenges – those of us who believe passionately in the importance of the european union – is that often people do not see the work that is done in parliament, the commission, the council as making any difference or being relevant to their everyday concerns about their quality of life and standard of living. therefore, it is very important, in the context not only of 2006 but also of the debate on the financial perspective for the years ahead, that we constantly have in mind the importance of linking our actions, our words and the decisions that we make with the centrality of making sure that we rebuild and strengthen public confidence and support in the whole function, the work and vision which underpins the european union. a very good place to start would be to reach in a mature way a consensual agreement on the 2006 budget. we have major challenges ahead, but we can bridge the gap on that issue – there are significant gaps in some of the budget headings, as we will hear in the debate this afternoon, and very strong differences of opinion about the best way forward. however, i believe that in the next few weeks we should be seeking to bridge those gaps. we should be seeking to achieve some level of consensus, which will inevitably require compromise. if we can do that, it will be a very important building block in terms of the challenges which lie ahead, in terms of the necessary reforms to the way that we budget and make decisions about the future. many of you will have been present when the prime minister of the united kingdom made his speech to parliament very early on in the presidency. i think there was general agreement among everybody present – whatever their political ideology, whatever their views – as he outlined the reform agenda and his determination that we achieve that in partnership, that his was a fair analysis of where europe is now and that now is the time to grasp the nettle and deal with some of the fundamental issues about the future nature of the european union and its relationship with its citizens. the 2006 budget may – in the context of that big-picture debate – feel like a relatively small issue. however, if we can reach some level of agreement, if we do our business. i am pleased, mr president, honourable members, ladies and gentlemen, to close my remarks and to commend the draft budget to the european parliament this afternoon.
