the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this report has been the subject of a very important and positive debate in committee, and i should like to begin by thanking all the members for this. the reasons for suggesting the introduction of a consolidated common tax base for companies operating in several countries of the union relate to the reduction of barriers to the completion of the internal market and are inspired by the lisbon strategy. this is for two reasons in particular. the first concerns the need to simplify and reduce the administrative and management costs for companies which today face 25 different tax bases and which will then be able to fulfil their tax obligations more easily, while also receiving an incentive to invest and operate in a european dimension and not only in a national one. the second reason is one of transparency, because the unification of tax bases will make opportunistic behaviour more difficult, since a common tax base will allow - while not interfering in any way with the levels of taxation in the different member states - to finally make the different levels of taxation fully legible and comparable. these two reasons, fully acknowledged by the experts and business representatives we heard during the drafting of the report, convinced a very large number of committee members. it is a very difficult operation, both politically and technically. the political difficulties are due to the fact that a number of countries - albeit fewer than a few years ago - are showing difficulties and reluctance to deal with taxation issues, even if in this case it is not about rates. the main technical difficulties are to be found in identifying a homogeneous basis of indicators for a common tax base. the commission has been working on this for some time and has set up technical groups. the commission's report is a welcome expression of our appreciation for the work of the commission, encouraging it, urging it and offering some guidance. the intention and commitment of the members of the committee was to promote a broad and strong statement by parliament, which i hope is possible, although this will of course involve some concessions and some discipline on the part of the political groups. taxation is a very difficult matter. it is no secret that the positions of the various groups and the various member states are very different. that is why we in the committee have drawn up compromise hypotheses which focus on the subject of the question, namely the consolidated common tax base, without going into the wider field of competition or tax convergence, which remains open and has not been dealt with here. this approach has enabled us to give substance to the report and to give some useful and precise indications. the report shall request the drawing up of a regulation, indicating the contents deemed necessary. it also provides for the possibility of using enhanced cooperation if unanimity cannot be reached, and for a gradual approach to the introduction of the common base, optional at the outset, with a mid-term assessment to consider whether a mandatory introduction phase should be followed. the subject we are presenting is therefore well defined, but it is nevertheless an important subject which i hope will be taken up by a large majority of parliament. for this reason, although i also share some of my own views in the amendments which have been tabled, i think it is essential to preserve the profile of the report in this debate and in the votes in the house, a balance achieved in committee which i believe is essential for the success of this initiative.

the commission's vice-president madam president, mr minister, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, if we are today on the verge of obtaining agreement with the council on such a sensitive proposal at second reading, it is primarily thanks to the excellent work, and i dare say to the perseverance, of your rapporteur, mrs wortmann-kool. let me, madam, congratulate you most warmly. i would like to recall the approach behind the proposal for a directive. the first thing to do is to find answers to the imbalance and the risk of inefficiency that the transport system in europe is facing today. these problems were identified in the white paper on the common transport policy. our response is that if transport users are progressively made to bear the costs of the transport they use, this will help to reduce pollution and congestion and to provide additional funding for investment in transport infrastructure. the text under discussion today amends the current directive dating from 1999, which regulates the application of tolls and user charges on europe's motorways. the current directive is both restrictive and ineffective. binding, since it prohibits the application of tolls on any road infrastructure other than motorways. moreover, it requires infrastructure costs to be the only element in the calculation of the toll amount. it is not effective, however, since it does not provide any methodology for implementing these provisions. the absence of a methodology for calculating infrastructure costs is detrimental to fair competition and favours discriminatory treatment of users. the commission has proposed several amendments to deal with this situation. first, geographical coverage applied to the whole transeuropean road network. secondly, a start - only a start, it is true, but a start nonetheless - of taking external costs into account: the framework for the practice of discounts, the introduction of the principle of allocating toll revenue. the council, mr minister, had more difficulty in reaching a decision, while parliament was able to deliver its opinion on first reading quickly. it took four council meetings before we could reach an agreement, and i, in turn, want to thank you. understandably, transit states are seeking to shift more of the external costs of road transport onto road users. the peripheral states want to ensure that transport plays its role as an integrator of their national economies into the single market, and this divergence of views between transit and peripheral states makes the discussion difficult, but it has also made it possible to find this compromise. since then, the three institutions have worked hard to reach agreement at second reading. significant improvements have been made thanks to the amendments of the european parliament and thanks to you, mrs wortmann-kool. the text now on the table is in line with the concerns which the commission has expressed in the form of statements. the first concerns the step you take on the path towards internalising external costs. the new directive will allow for the partial internalisation of external costs and will allow for the use of overlaying in mountain areas. the revenue from this surplus should be used to finance alternative transport infrastructure. the new directive will also allow for greater variation in tolls, depending on the pollution of vehicles or congestion on the roads. finally, as regards the analysis of the internalisation of external costs, i am pleased to say that the modelling and impact analyses requested by parliament can be developed and published by the commission in the next two years. on this basis, the commission will be able to assess the need for further community action. the second concern is the geographical coverage of this directive. the new directive will allow member states to apply tolls and user charges to all roads. and your amendments are designed to ensure that the application of tolls by member states will be based on clear principles for the calculation of tolls so that they are fair, non-discriminatory and in line with community legislation. as regards the possibility of overcrowding in urban areas, the compromise you propose is reasonable. it is perfectly clear that if member states wish to introduce urban toll systems to reduce pollution and congestion, they are free to do so, and in this respect the example of london seems to me to be quite interesting. finally, on the question of vehicles covered by the future directive, you have defined the deadlines and the exceptions to the inclusion of vehicles over 3.5 tonnes in the scope of the directive. these are sensible proposals which will make it possible to implement the directive better. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, the commission can accept without any difficulty parliament's amendments, which reflect the compromise negotiated between our three institutions.

charge goods vehicles down to 3.5 tonnes and not just vehicles of more than 12 tonnes; benefit from much more scope to vary tolls to influence hauliers’ behaviour to reduce congestion and pollution; impose a mark-up in mountainous regions to combat congestion and pollution and raise new funds for major trans-european network projects. the directive will provide for the commission to develop a model for the assessment of external costs in no longer than two years. this model, together with an impact assessment, will, if appropriate, allow the commission to bring forward a proposal for further amendment of the eurovignette directive. i am sure that i do not need to say that these are important achievements on a new directive which will balance the interests of the peripheral states and transit countries, hauliers, environmentalists and, most of all, will benefit the citizens of europe. i should like to congratulate all concerned once again for managing to find a compromise that satisfies both the council and parliament. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's air transport policy is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. this is a situation which unfortunately occurs with alarming frequency and which requires the adoption of this regulation as a matter of urgency. thanks to the efforts of the rapporteur, mr evans, and the willingness of the council and the commission, we have reached a good compromise which will allow us to approve the rules at first reading and to implement them quickly. this regulation is important for disabled and elderly passengers, as it guarantees a number of fundamental rights: first, it provides for the right to free assistance and prohibits the refusal of boarding to passengers with reduced mobility. this measure will put an end to abuses and discrimination. secondly, the airport operator is the only contact person with general responsibility for the service to which passengers can turn, and it will also allow airlines which have provided quality assistance to date to continue to provide the service, provided they comply with the standards set out in the regulation. finally, rules are established for equal assistance for all, regardless of the size of the airport. assistance will have to be provided by the external arrival points at the airport and not just by the check-in as is the case today. compensation will be provided for the loss or damage of wheelchairs and other equipment, and mandatory training for staff responsible for assistance will be provided. the information will be available in formats that are accessible to all and privacy will be guaranteed. these are fundamental guarantees for the protection of the right to mobility without discrimination and therefore an important step forward in the defence of the rights of the individual whose european parliament is the guarantor.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking mr koterec for his work. this is less state aid and more targeted aid in order to respond effectively to the challenges posed by economic globalisation, enlargement and the need to boost competitiveness in the union. however, there is a risk that some territories will be penalised: state aid must be used to promote competitiveness and innovation, research and development, throughout the european union. in this context, it would be particularly desirable to create a transitional mechanism for statistical regions. i therefore ask the commission to take account of the new wording of paragraph 7 of the text of the koterec report, as approved by the regi committee. and i call on the european commission to take note and to act accordingly, and to take greater account of the unemployment rate of a region in determining its status.
state aid is targeted at particularly disadvantaged regions and contributes, even more specifically than other policies, to the achievement of the lisbon, gothenburg and barcelona objectives. they are therefore an important tool for the states to help the most disadvantaged regions, such as those affected by the so-called statistical effect of enlargement, or less-favoured areas, such as islands or mountainous areas. reducing and better targeting of state aid is essential for effective competition, but attention must be paid to the parameters proposed by the new guidelines. they impose too high differentials between the 15 and the new member states, generating a waste of incentives which hinders further results in terms of attracting new businesses, leads to a displacement of non-competitive businesses which can only survive through subsidies, and creates surreptitious competition between the poorest areas of europe. it is therefore necessary to restore more moderate intensities and to reduce the gap between the ceilings of the regions whose development is lagging behind. finally, the 'flexibility' of aid to large enterprises should be emphasised.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as is customary at the beginning of the vote, the rapporteur-general has made some technical corrections. i would like to make a few comments on the amendments which have been tabled. but first i would like to thank you, because this has been a difficult but very satisfying job. i would therefore like to take this opportunity to express my warm thanks to all my colleagues on the committee on budgets, to mr lewandowski, the chairman, the coordinators and staff of the political groups, the secretariat and all its members, and first of all to the administrator who has given me the constant, loyal and competent help of mr richard wester, a help which has been positively combined with the meticulous expertise of my assistant, mrs annalisa gliubizzi. i also thank all of you, starting with president borrell, who has followed all the steps of the procedure closely, and of course all the colleagues who have contributed ideas and proposals, and who i hope will also contribute to a good result today by voting for me and honouring me with their trust. ladies and gentlemen, this is a very good result, a counter-trend, and all the institutions should be commended for it, but i am proud to say that it is above all our parliament. i hope that this result will open the minds of those who still do not want to understand how high the cost of non-europe is. the technical requirements to be met are the following: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would point out that this is technically possible only for those budget lines on which there was already an amendment tabled by parliament. where this is not the case, we call on the commission to submit a proposal for a transfer as soon as possible. the relevant headings are 02 01 04 04; 04 01 04 05; 04 05 01; 04 05 02; 04 05 03; 09 03 01; 11 07 01; 24 02 02. secondly, the part of amendment no 209 relating to line 19 08 02 01 on the meda programme is approved for an amount of eur 25 056 550. this amendment is covered by the vote on block 1. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after these technical corrections, i propose that we proceed to the vote and i also take this opportunity to wish you all the best and warmest of happy holidays. (applause) i would like to thank
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would just like to say that if this amendment were to be rejected, we would be going beyond the ceiling agreed with the council and would therefore have some problems with the procedure. i therefore rely on the colleagues' sense of responsibility. (parliament adopted the legislative resolution)
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is really a minor adjustment, just to make it clear that the letter of amendment was made in accordance with point two, that is to say, the agreement between parliament and the council, but it is really a formal adjustment which does not affect the substance in the slightest.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to point out that we voted for the compromise amendment tabled last night by the green and socialist groups, to which i personally contributed, although i believe that this amendment is weaker than the text of article 21, which we helped to draft. we voted for this amendment in the interests of children, because we wanted this parliament to speak with one voice, strong and convinced, to send a message to romania so that the problem of intercountry adoptions can be solved successfully. we do not expect this to happen before christmas, but we hope that it will happen so that these children - who have a right to a family as a priority, as is enshrined in all the rules in force at international level - can be reunited with their parents. this is a human right, a fundamental right which parliament wishes to emphasize to romania, because among the various things it will have to do to conform to the european acquis, it will first of all have to ensure respect for human rights, in this case the right of children to have the joy and happiness of a family.
